news.title: Report — Democrat Candidates Avoid Kamala Harris as Midterms Loom: 'She Is a Huge Liability'
news.text:
Some Democrat candidates are reportedly unsure how close they should get to former Vice President Kamala Harris (D), while one megadonor advised them to keep their distance.

Many of those candidates have won her support, but some do not have a favorable view of her after she lost to President Donald Trump in 2024, the Hill reported Saturday.

“Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek (D) told reporters this week he didn’t want Harris to campaign for him as he pursues a Senate seat this cycle — a sentiment Iowa gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand, the state’s auditor, also shared about Harris and former President Biden,” the outlet said. “Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s (D-AK) Senate campaign also voiced frustration after Harris’s PAC issued a fundraising email for the red-state Democrat earlier this month.”

There has been talk of her trying to take the White House again in 2028, and Harris was reported to have been privately contacting progressive Democrats, pro-Palestinian activists, former aides, and other party figures before a possible run for president, according to Breitbart News.

The Hill also referred to Democrats in Michigan where the race for the U.S. Senate is heating up and where some of them believe she could hurt their chances.

Democrat megadonor John Morgan said, “She is a huge liability” and those who have a chance at winning needed to stay far away from her.

“‘Look what happened in Alaska,’ he said, referring to Harris’s PAC appeal on behalf of Peltola and how Republicans have used it to tie Harris to the candidate,” the article read.

In June, a poll showed Vice President JD Vance (R) and Harris dominating within their own parties among potential 2028 candidates, according to Breitbart News.

Rep. Mark Harris (R-NC) told Breitbart News Saturday in April that the prospect of Harris running for president in 2028 may certainly “help” Republicans before the midterms “because it reminds the people of what they rejected in 2024.”

news.title: Newsmax Host Carl Higbie Deletes Jelly Roll Music After Country Star Makes Trump Weight Jokes
news.text: Conservative TV host Carl Higbie used his Newsmax show in New York on Thursday night to delete Jelly Roll tracks from his phone on live television, lashing out at the country star after Jelly Roll mocked President Donald Trump's weight during a guest-host spot on Jimmy Kimmel Live!Jelly Roll, who has long tried to stay out of overt politics, stepped into late-night this week as a guest host on ABC's Jimmy Kimmel Live! and promptly detonated his uneasy truce with parts of his MAGA fanbase.In his opening monologue, he cracked a run of jokes about Trump, targeting everything from the president's size to his record on gas prices, healthcare and the war in Iran. The reaction online was instant and, in right-wing circles at least, pretty mad.Carl Higbie, Jelly Roll and a Very Public 'Unfollow'Jelly Roll used his own body transformation as material, telling the ABC audience he had lost around 300 pounds and quipping that he had 'lost an entire Donald Trump.' He went further, addressing the president directly in one gag: 'Mr President, from one fat pig to another, take it from me that physical fitness is very important.'At another point, he pushed the line again, saying viewers could argue about whether Trump was 'mentally fit' but could probably agree that he is 'certainly not physically fit.' That kind of fat-on-fat humour, as Jelly Roll framed it, did not land with everyone. 'I thought fat-on-fat crime was OK!' he later said, doubling down rather than backing off.Higbie, a former Navy SEAL and staunch Trump loyalist, clearly put himself in the offended camp. On his Newsmax programme Carl Higbie Frontline, he told viewers Jelly Roll had been a personal favourite until the late-night monologue triggered what he called a 'culture clash' over the president. He accused the singer of abandoning his long‑held decision to avoid politics and of 'coming in hot with Trump jokes.''Jelly Roll, who was previously a favourite of mine, he's been filling in for Jimmy Kimmel this week,' Higbie said. 'And after intentionally staying out of politics for like his whole career, he decided to come in hot with Trump jokes, calling him a fat pig, and he's not exactly a calendar model himself.'Higbie then rolled clips from Jimmy Kimmel Live! showing some of Jelly Roll's punchlines. In one, the musician tried to widen the frame beyond Trump as an individual. 'Any US president should be able to handle a few jokes, right?' Jelly Roll said. 'They should also be able to handle gas prices, healthcare, and the occasional international conflict.'He also addressed the brewing backlash among Trump supporters watching from home. 'Look, y'all, I get it. Some people are mad at me for goofing on Trump,' Jelly Roll said. 'But if you wanted me to make jokes about Kamala Harris, you should have voted for her.'Jelly Roll Pushes Back as MAGA Turns on HimThe real flashpoint came when Jelly Roll spoke directly to his own audience, acknowledging that some fans had vowed to stop streaming his work after the monologue. His response was blunt. 'So for those who threatened to stop listening to my music based on my comments last night, I just wanna say with conviction, go right ahead,' he said.That line seemed to egg on critics more than calm them. Higbie seized on it as a kind of dare. Reaching into his pocket mid‑segment, he pulled out his phone and told viewers: 'Go ahead. OK, dude. OK. I'll be deleting his music as we speak.' Newsmax cameras zoomed in on his screen as he deleted Jelly Roll's track I Am Not OK from his Apple Music library.'I held him in high regards until then. Come on, dude,' Higbie added, visibly irritated. It was a small act, a single swipe on a smartphone, but it played as a tidy bit of culture‑war theatre, the sort of stuff US cable news now runs on.Higbie's reaction also landed in a particular political context. He was appointed by Trump as external affairs chief at the Corporation for National and Community Service during the president's first term, according to federal records, before resigning in 2018 after racist remarks he had made in 2013 resurfaced.He has since worked with pro‑Trump outfits including America First Policies and Great America PAC, which helps explain why a country singer's late‑night jokes could quickly turn into prime‑time content.MAGA Backlash Spills Beyond NewsmaxThe anger did not stop with Higbie's performative delete. Jelly Roll's monologue drew heat across Republican circles and from some elected officials. Florida's Chief Financial Officer, Jimmy Patronis, posted on X that the musician 'is 100% not welcomed to Florida's panhandle,' underlining how local politicians are now willing to treat late‑night comedy as a litmus test for loyalty.Jelly Roll, for his part, had largely sidestepped explicit political talk in interviews before taking the Jimmy Kimmel Live! gig. His decision to lean into Trump jokes on network television marked a clear shift, intentional or not, in how openly he is prepared to signal his views.What happens next is harder to pin down. There is no polling to show how many fans will actually stop listening, and no clear evidence yet that his streaming numbers have taken a serious hit.What is clear is that a guest monologue on a late‑night chat show has spiralled into a familiar fight over respect, loyalty and who gets to crack jokes about the president. One entertainer tried to poke fun at the most powerful man in the country.Another entertainer‑turned‑host responded by wiping a playlist and turning it into a segment. That is where American politics lives now, at least for one news cycle.

news.title: Trump confirms Pentagon plans for 25th anniversary of 9/11 attacks, disputes report on Ground Zero absence
news.text: President Donald Trump said Friday that he's going to be at the Pentagon to mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorists attacks. A reporter on Friday asked the president why he was not planning to be in New York for the somber occasion. "Because I'm going to the Pentagon," Trump shouted to the press at Joint Base Andrews. On Thursday, The New York Times reported that Trump was not planning to attend the ceremony at Ground Zero, where the Twin Towers came down, because he wouldn't be allowed to give a speech. The annual event has banned politicians from speaking since 2012. I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11. PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES When asked about the Times report, a White House spokeswoman called Trump a "proud New Yorker." "President Trump has spoken about his own experiences watching the horrific events of September 11, 2001. On the 25th anniversary of this tragic day, the President will remember those who were killed at the hands of evil terrorists, honor their loved ones, and pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line to rescue their fellow Americans," White House principal deputy press secretary Anna Kelly said in a statement to Fox News. "The vice president is still traveling to NYC and all three sites will be represented with administration officials in attendance," a White House official said, referring to the three Sept. 11 attack sites in Manhattan, at the Pentagon and near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, where United Airlines Flight 93 crashed. After TMZ posted on X that Trump was "snubbing" the Ground Zero ceremony, White House communications director Steven Cheung fired back. "FAKE NEWS," Cheung wrote. Trump lambasted the reporter behind in the Times article, writing on Truth Social Friday that she "made up a story that on September 11th, I’m not going to the World Trade Center, in New York City, because they won’t let me make a speech, and I’m going to the Pentagon in D.C., because I’m a featured speaker." "This is more Corrupt News, I’ve been to New York many times over the years, and no one ever speaks, it’s a 'solemn ceremony!'" Trump wrote in part. Trump said, "I would love not to speak, because I’m speaking all the time, and this is a day to remember the victims, and their beautiful family members." Last year, Trump also chose to speak at the Pentagon for the 24th anniversary of 9/11, though he traveled to New York City later in the day to attend a Yankees game. JUDGE THROWS OUT KHALID SHEIKH MOHAMMED'S 9/11 CONFESSION IN ALREADY LONG WAIT FOR TRIAL The last time he attended the Ground Zero ceremony was in 2024, when he was the Republican presidential nominee. He was there alongside then-President Joe Biden and his election rival, then-Vice President Kamala Harris. Trump also did not attend the Ground Zero ceremony during his first term. He spoke at the Pentagon in 2017, then alternated in subsequent years between commemorations there and at the site in Pennsylvania. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Nearly 3,000 people were killed in the terrorist attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, when al-Qaeda hijackers crashed three commercial airliners into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon. Hijackers also seized United Airlines Flight 93, but passengers fought back before the plane crashed in Pennsylvania. The 9/11 attacks, which remain the deadliest in the nation's history, prompted the invasion of Afghanistan and helped usher in the broader War on Terror, which later included the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq. Fox News' Patrick Ward contributed to this report.
news.summary: President Donald Trump said he will be at the Pentagon. A White House official said Vice President JD Vance will travel to New York for the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks.

news.title: Why don’t celebrities go away anymore?
news.text:
Do me a favor. Picture MTV’s “Total Request Live” at the height of its powers. Carson Daly shouting to be heard over an audience of excited adolescents. Feuds stoked daily between teenyboppers like NSYNC and teenymoshers like Limp Bizkit. Overflow crowds standing on Broadway to scream at the slightest glimpse of a chart-topper in the second-story window of New York City’s One Astor Place. 

Now, imagine all that delirium, sign-waving and call-in voting was in service of pushing Art Garfunkel to the pinnacle of the premier music video countdown. Ridiculous, right? Garfunkel’s tender folk couldn’t be farther from the chrome-coated zeitgeist of the turn of the last century. The musicians who supplanted the East Village folkies were by that time dinosaurs themselves, having been rendered extinct by pop permutations several times over. Daly’s daily countdown was about an eternal present, a shiny go-go now that had no time for the dour, mildewy Neil Young worship of the early ‘90s, to say nothing of the decades prior. 

But that chorus of screams for the latest from Garfunkel, the man behind “All I Know,” shouldn’t sound so odd to us. After all, we’re about as removed from Destiny Child’s first hit (1997’s “No, No, No”) as the “TRL” audience was from “Bridge Over Troubled Water.” The seismic shifts in pop culture made something like Garfunkelpalooza feel silly, while culture publications and the wider social internet will regularly reshape entire weeks around the release of Beyoncé’s latest album. 

She’s not unique in that regard. Taylor Swift launched a years-long stadium tour nearly two full decades after her first chart-topper. Before it ended in December 2024, the “Eras Tour” rearranged cities that it visited and rejiggered the way that pop fans discussed album cycles and stylistic shifts. 

The advent of streaming in the late 2000s replaced syndication with on-demand, binge rewatches, extending the half-life of television toward the infinite. Even the smallest side characters were gifted their own spin-offs in the streaming service-boosted age of marketable intellectual property. Disney got to work making spin-offs of spin-offs of stories about a bounty hunter who had around 10 minutes of screen time in the original Star Wars trilogy. Small-screen stars leaned into the long tail of their most-famous roles, launching rewatch podcasts for everything from “The West Wing” and “The Office” to “Beverly Hills, 90210” and “Hot in Cleveland,” further extending their 15 minutes of fame. 

Simon Reynolds was one of the first commentators to notice, and pathologized the backwards-looking, stalled-out culture as “retromania” in 2010. Over a decade later, the New York Times thought the problem hadn’t been resolved, wondering whether we were living through a cultural “standstill.” Critic W. David Marx, looking to sum up the curiously stagnant opening decades of the 21st century, cribbed a phrase from one of its enduring icons for the title of his book “Blank Space.” 

The last 20 years, Marx said, have been one big “lowest-common-denominator fight for attention,” meaning it was easier than ever to remain a public figure and make money off the resulting eyeballs. He accused the forces of financialization and social media for creating a world where “fame and infamy” were “indistinguishable.” 

In 2026, you can see this play out most obviously via former NBA players like Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White. Picked near the top of their respective drafts, both men crafted passable but underwhelming careers in the league. Where prior players would be happy to head home and count their money, popping up on occasion in documentaries to discuss the difficulties of guarding Lebron James, Freedom and Royce have delayed their natural decline into trivia by staging a transgender panic around the WNBA. 

Freedom and White clearly see a post-league career in playing into the worst of conservative media’s impulses. To that end, they’ve both become outspoken advocates against trans athletes playing in the WNBA. Realizing there are no trans athletes in the WNBA currently in the WNBA or entering the draft, they resolved to become the issue and declared themselves women who wish to play in the league. In the weeks since, Freedom has taken to his role as a supposed protector of women by verbally harassing current WNBA players while sitting courtside. Knowing that Freedom won’t be deterred from his second-act as a bigot no matter how many arenas he’s thrown out of, it’s hard to get past the idea that we’re playing these arguments out in a void.

Politics as a whole is hardly exempt from these decades of wheel-spinning. The oddly elongated two term-presidency of Donald Trump, a petty man who rarely fails to bring his old grudges, has turned U.S. global and national politics into one big score to settle. The president never got over his loss to Joe Biden in 2020, and the Democrats never got over theirs to Trump four years before. New wars and new horrors carried out by the Trump administration can’t shake the feeling that we’re having the same old arguments.

As the 2028 election cycle draws near — if recent history is a guide, candidates are likely to begin officially declaring their candidacies in early 2027 — many of the Democratic Party’s contenders can draw a direct line to the presidency of Barack Obama. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and former Vice President Kamala Harris look all but certain to join the race . . . again. Expect them to run along similar moderate lines as before, pitching themselves as the sensible choice and avoiding too much chatter about their previous losses.

Former Housing and Urban Development Secretary Andrew Cuomo didn’t serve in the Obama administration, but as New York’s former governor during the bulk of the Obama years, he is inextricably tied to the era. Despite his loss in the 2025 New York City mayoral race and credible allegations of sexual harassment, he is making unsettling noises about the race, and is apparently hoping to represent the party’s establishment wing, even though his constituency now amounts to almost no one.

Obama’s former chief of staff Rahm Emanuel is old enough to collect Social Security. But reports say he’s stress-testing campaign staffers’ tolerance for colorful language in the hopes of running as a bulwark against candidates who oppose U.S. aid to Israel. 

All this is playing out as Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer is capping a career of failing to meet the moment by hanging on to his seat and leadership position for dear life — and hamstringing the party’s progressive youth movement in the process. 

An older, careerist Democratic Party creates a perspective problem that’s hard to overcome. Each passing year carries office holders further away from the median age of their voters and further calcifies their opinions on the way politics gets done. You can see it every time Schumer rolls over for the Trumpist GOP, operating as if the mutual back-scratching vibes weren’t saged from the Capitol Dome the second it was breached by Trump-supporting rioters. 

But away from the party’s power center, the first flashes of something exciting and new have begun to appear.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and his seemingly supernatural competence at both city management and marketing, has laid a blueprint for kitchen-table progressives looking to bust out of the Trump-era holding pattern. The Florida Democratic Party might be running an ex-Republican for governor again, but the Senate candidacy of democratic socialist Angie Nixon gives some hope for forward-thinking campaigns going forward. Any honest rundown of 2028 hopefuls has to include first-wave Sanders-ite Alexandria Ocasio Cortez, the strongest indication yet that we might break free from the long shadow of 2016. 

A better world, where we never have to type out a name as unpleasant as Gavin Newsom again, just might be possible.

news.title: AOC Within Striking Distance of Beating Vance In New 2028 Poll
news.text: Democratic Representative of New York, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, is within striking distance of Republican Vice President JD Vance in an early hypothetical 2028 presidential contest, new polling shows, although neither party has chosen a nominee. Key Points What To Know Vance led Ocasio-Cortez by 3.3 points in Quantus Insights’ national survey of likely voters conducted from August 26 to 28. Their narrow early hypothetical matchup contrasts with clearer primary leads for Buttigieg and Vance inside their respective parties. Nothing changes electorally yet, but the findings offer an early measure of both parties’ possible coalitions before the 2028 campaign takes shape. Why It Matters A national vote remains more than two years away, and hypothetical polling this early measures current political appeal rather than forecasting a nominee or the eventual result. Still, Ocasio-Cortez’s proximity to Vance suggests a potentially competitive contest despite stark differences between their demographic bases. Poll Details Quantus Insights surveyed 1,200 likely voters through SMS-to-mobile interviews between August 26 and 28. The poll used voter-file information and weighted results by sex, age, race, education, party, and metro type; its design-adjusted margin of error was plus or minus 3.2 percentage points at the 95 percent confidence level. Subgroup margins were larger. Because the 3.3-point candidate gap is almost the same size as the full survey’s stated margin of error, the result describes a close race rather than a secure Vance advantage. Both Candidates Are Keeping Their Options Open Neither Ocasio-Cortez nor Vance has declared a 2028 campaign. Asked on ABC’s This Week on August 9 whether she might run for president, Ocasio-Cortez said she was focused on the midterms and her current congressional campaign but added: “I haven’t ruled out the possibility.” When asked about a potential challenge to Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, whose seat is also on the ballot in 2028, she said “anything is possible at this juncture.” Her political operation is also undergoing personnel changes. Axios reported on August 28 that longtime campaign manager and senior adviser Oliver Hidalgo-Wohlleben would leave in September, with longtime aide Fiorella Bini taking over as interim campaign manager. Former aides Aya Saed and Tanushri Shankar-Ross have returned in senior roles, while chief of staff Mike Casca, a veteran of Bernie Sanders’ 2020 presidential operation, has taken on a larger portfolio. Axios placed the changes against Ocasio-Cortez’s expected decision between a presidential campaign and a possible Senate run. Personnel moves alone do not demonstrate that a campaign is imminent. They do, however, add practical context to speculation surrounding a politician who has publicly declined to close off either route. Vance has adopted a similarly noncommittal timetable. In a June 14 interview with CBS Sunday Morning, he said he and his wife, Usha Vance, would discuss what came next for their family after the 2026 midterms. “I have no doubt that the president of the United States is going to be very supportive of anything that I ultimately decide to do,” Vance said. “But we really just haven’t talked about what that thing will be.” He added that he did not want thoughts about “a future job” to make him “a worse vice president.” Newsweek reached out to Ocasio-Cortez and Vance for further comment via email and website contact form, respectively, on Saturday morning. AOC-Vance Matchup Reveals Two Different Coalitions Ocasio-Cortez led among women, receiving 48.7 percent against Vance’s 37.1 percent. Men divided in the opposite direction, backing Vance by 53.9 percent to 34.4 percent. Age created another sharp split. Voters aged 18 to 29 favored Ocasio-Cortez by 53.4 percent to 24.9 percent, while those aged 65 and older preferred Vance by 51.6 percent to 37 percent. The Republican also led among voters aged 45 to 64, whereas the 30-to-44 group narrowly favored the Democrat. Education followed a similar pattern. Ocasio-Cortez led college graduates by 48 percent to 37.6 percent and postgraduate voters by 48.6 percent to 26.4 percent. Vance held a 52.9 percent to 36 percent advantage among people whose highest qualification was high school or some college. Geography reinforced the contrast. Urban voters backed Ocasio-Cortez 53.6 percent to 32.6 percent, while Vance led in suburbs, rural areas and towns. Among racial and ethnic groups, the Democrat led Black, Hispanic and Asian respondents; the Republican carried white voters. Results based on fewer than 30 respondents were marked by the pollster as directional only. Buttigieg Leads The 2028 Democratic Primary Buttigieg registered 25.7 percent among 515 strong and leaning Democrats, followed by Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia at 21.3 percent and Ocasio-Cortez at 15.3 percent. Another 19.4 percent were undecided. Former Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris received 8.1 percent, while California Governor Gavin Newsom stood at 7.1 percent. The ordering differed by partisan intensity: Buttigieg led strong Democrats with 28.4 percent, but Ossoff topped leaning Democrats at 33.5 percent. That division matters because it shows no single candidate yet combining the party’s most committed supporters with its less firmly attached voters. Vance Leads 2028 Republican Primary Vance took 41 percent among 473 strong and leaning Republicans, placing him 11.9 points ahead of Marco Rubio, who received 29.1 percent. Donald Trump Jr. followed with 9.1 percent, Ron DeSantis had 6.3 percent and Tucker Carlson registered 0.3 percent. Ten percent were undecided. Intensity again changed the picture. Vance commanded 48.8 percent among strong Republicans, but Rubio led leaning Republicans by 39 percent to 27.2 percent. Wider Political Environment Favors Democrats The same survey placed Democrats ahead on the generic congressional ballot, 49.7 percent to 42.8 percent, with 7.5 percent undecided. President Donald Trump’s job approval stood at 41.9 percent, compared with 56.7 percent disapproval. Those figures provide important context for the presidential test. Ocasio-Cortez’s showing may reflect both personal support and a national environment that was favorable to Democrats when voters were interviewed. What Happens Next One survey cannot establish the shape of an election years away. The clearest next signal will be whether future polls reproduce Ocasio-Cortez’s demographic coalition and narrow deficit, or whether the result proves specific to this sample and political moment. Contact Newsweek editor on this story: Edward Pearcey.

news.title: Judge Rejects Trump Bid to Shift Manhattan Case to Federal Court
news.text:
President Donald Trump has again fallen short in his effort to move his long-running New York City criminal case out of state court and into the federal system, after a Manhattan federal judge rejected his latest bid.

“The grounds for a second removal cited by Defendant, Donald J. Trump, are neither new nor legally sufficient,” the judge wrote in a 35-page order issued Friday. “He has failed to show good cause and diligence. His motion for leave to file a second notice of removal is denied.”

Trump has repeatedly tried, both before and after his conviction on 34 felony counts, to shift the local prosecution into federal court. Each attempt has failed.

The federal fight before U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein, who was appointed by President Bill Clinton, began in May 2023 when Trump first filed a notice seeking removal.

After an intense round of briefing and motions, Hellerstein ruled against Trump in July 2023 and returned the matter to New York Supreme Court in New York County, the official name of Manhattan’s trial-level court.

Trump’s appeals did not change the outcome. In May 2024, the 45th president was convicted. By late August 2024, he had filed a second notice of removal. About two months later, Trump defeated Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election and subsequently returned to the White House as the 47th president.

As that renewed removal effort remained unresolved, Trump’s sentencing loomed over the case. The matter ultimately ended in the then-president-elect’s favor when New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan imposed an “unconditional discharge.” That outcome left Trump’s conviction for falsifying business records intact but imposed no punishment or other adverse legal consequences tied to the hush-money case involving payments made to Stormy Daniels before the 2016 election.

Between the election and sentencing decision, the district court denied the removal notice again — and denied a motion to stay the ruling. The case then went up the appellate ladder and came before the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in June 2025.

In November 2025, the appellate court sent the case back to the district court to reconsider the president’s motion in light of the U.S. Supreme Court’s landmark opinion on presidential immunity.

Now, Hellerstein has considered months’ worth of motions and hearings — and is still resolutely not convinced.

“President Trump must show that ‘he acted diligently and without undue delay to remove the case based on’ new grounds, here, principally the issuance of the United States Supreme Court’s decision in Trump v. United States, in order to ‘show good cause for the untimely filing at issue,'” the court’s order reads. “He fails to do so.”

The judge recites the timelines of the various cases, noting that Trump “made a strategic decision” to use presidential immunity claims as a defense in his criminal trial instead of as a removal basis during the trial. Then, Trump used immunity claims as a basis to dismiss after the trial — again not as a basis for removal.

“Finally, 64 days later, and when it became apparent that the New York court likely intended to deny his motion to dismiss and sentence him two days after, Trump filed his motion in federal court,” the judge explains.

But by then it was too late for such a removal claim, the judge found.

“A party seeking to remove must do so promptly no later than 30 days after arraignment or any time before trial, whichever is earlier,” the order continues. “If he misses this window, he can seek leave to remove despite his lateness by showing ‘good cause.’ But he cannot play one court against another; he cannot seek victory in one court, and then, when it becomes apparent that the court will rule against him, seek to remove his case to another court.”

Hellerstein cites precedent to note that the removal statute does not mean “a party may experiment” in state court and then “transfer it to the federal court” if the experiment fails.

But that is admittedly what Trump and his legal team did here.

“At oral argument before the Court of Appeals, Trump’s counsel acknowledged ‘he could have sought removal immediately following the Supreme Court’s decision,'” the order goes on. “He instead elected to litigate immunity in state court.”

The judge notes “Trump himself recognizes” the second removal bid only came after it was clear immunity would fail in Empire State court.

“Trump seeks a ‘second bite at the apple,’ a result the law disfavors,” Hellerstein continues. “Trump’s delay in filing for removal constitutes a ‘quintessential strategic decision,’ and the ‘fact that he later came to view that decision as a poor one is not sufficient.”

The judge also said the lengthy gulf before filing was “inconsistent with good cause” in and of itself.

“The U.S. Supreme Court issued its decision July 1, 2024,” Hellerstein went on. “It took 64 more days for Trump to move in this court for leave to remove on September 3, 2024. I hold that President Trump failed to show good cause.”

news.title: A record 8 Black candidates for governor are running in 2026
news.text:
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore is running for reelection and is rumored to be a 2028 Democratic presidential contender, but he has taken on another initiative in 2026: electing more Black governors. 

Moore, 47, is one of just three Black Americans ever elected as a state's chief executive in a country that is 14% Black, but a roster of politically and geographically diverse candidates could triple that number.

At least eight Black gubernatorial nominees, including Moore, are among a bipartisan cast on the ballot this fall.

"I became the first in my state's history and now only the third elected in the history of America, and that is a bit indicting when you consider the fact that we have a country that's now 250 years old," Moore, the newly minted chair of the National Governors Association, told USA TODAY in an interview.

Moore, who had no electoral experience before running for governor, may be joined by swing-state Democrats including Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley in Wisconsin and Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, in Georgia.

The Republican Party has their own list of history-making contenders. Rep. Byron Donalds, a staunch Trump ally, will likely become the first Black governor of Florida, and Rep. John James is the Michigan gubernatorial GOP nominee in a competitive contest this November.

Wes Moore didn't want combat with Trump. But he's embracing the fight.

Democratic South Carolina state Rep. Jermaine Johnson and Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth, a Republican, are also running for governor as longshot candidates.

'My job is not to become the first'

Since the Civil Rights Movement of the 1960s, Black Democrats have been far more successful in majority-Black districts than in statewide elections with mostly White electorates. In many states, Black voters are a major component of the Democratic primary electorate, but now all the Black gubernatorial nominees must appeal to largely White electorates in their general election battles.

Black Republicans, of whom there have been far fewer in Congress, often represent districts where the majority of their constituency is White.

Jasmine Carrera Smith, a George Washington University expert on electability among Black voters, said Black gubernatorial candidates have had outsized success this cycle but continue to be underrepresented overall.

In November 1989, American history was made when Virginia elected Douglass Wilder as governor – but he only served four years because state law prevents governors there from seeking consecutive terms in office. Two decades later, in 2006, Deval Patrick was elected governor of Massachusetts. Moore was elected governor of Maryland more than 15 years later, in 2022.

Then-Lt. Gov. David Paterson became New York's first Black governor in 2008 when Gov. Eliot Spitzer resigned following a prostitution scandal. Paterson, a Democrat, later faced allegations of impropriety as well and withdrew from the 2010 race for governor.

Now 95, Wilder could live to see several Black candidates elected governor.

Crowley leads WI governor race, Hong supporters backing him, poll says

In addition to Crowley and Ford having strong chances, Florida is likely to elect Donalds as the successor to Gov. Ron DeSantis.

But Donalds has had to face what was considered by some to be a race-based attack when James Fishback, a Republican primary opponent, called the congressman a "slave to donors."

Black candidates face major tests in two key swing states

In Wisconsin, Crowley won a heated primary over a democratic socialist, in part on the strength of his support among Black voters. He now must court the general electorate in a state of nearly 6 million people that is 85% White – a challenge Black politicians often face, and which many address by de-emphasizing race.

"My job is not to become the first," Crowley, 40, told USA TODAY. "My job is to make sure that young people all across the state can see themselves in me and understand that there are many more opportunities that they'll have access to in the future for themselves."

Crowley, a married father of three daughters, is currently favored to replace his mentor, Gov. Tony Evers. The state's popular chief executive endorsed Crowley, who reentered the race after Evers' lieutenant governor dropped out amid a scandal and during rising concerns about state Rep. Francesca Hong's electability.

Crowley was first elected to the State Assembly in 2016 and served two terms.

Voting ends in Upper Midwest primaries, a test of progressive energy and Trump's influence

He then beat a more progressive, non-Black Democratic legislator in a close 2020 race for Milwaukee County executive – a result repeated this month when he won the state's Democratic primary over Hong, an Asian American state representative from Madison.

Hong made several gaffes that attracted national intention, including a 2020 tweet that Thanksgiving is "celebrating colonialism."

Crowley's general election opponent is Rep. Tom Tiffany, a member of the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus. Tiffany lags behind in general election polling, but major statewide elections in Wisconsin are typically decided by around 1 percentage point.

Georgia, another swing state, will also test Black candidates' sway.

Both Crowley and Bottoms have experience as chief executives, which may give them an edge compared to past Black nominees in their respective states who did not. Mandela Barnes, a former lieutenant governor who lost to Sen. Ron Johnson in 2022, was previously a state legislator. Georgia's former Democratic House speaker, Stacey Abrams, was also a lawmaker before she lost races to Gov. Brian Kemp in 2018 and 2022.

Black candidates often lose in difficult areas for their parties

Bottoms' quest to succeed Kemp, the state's Republican governor, who is term limited, will likely lead to a close race. Her opponent Rick Jackson, a health care CEO and billionaire, is well-funded, and she faces questions about a crime spike during her pandemic-era tenure in Atlanta.

If elected, Bottoms would make history as the country's first Black woman to serve as governor, after Abrams failed to cross the finish line in two consecutive contests.

Meet the young Black MAGA fans trying to grow Trump's movement

Paru Shah, an expert on politics at Rutgers University, said the number of Black gubernatorial candidates this cycle will test longstanding arguments about electability that have often faced nonwhite contenders. Shah said that while identity does factor into political outcomes, voters typically focus first on party preference.

"It ends up being that they lose in places that it would have been difficult for a Democrat to win anyway, but then the narrative is not that Democrats can't win, it's that Black women can't win, or Black men can't win," Shah said.

She pointed to Abrams' losses in Georgia, a swing state that Trump lost in 2020 to former President Joe Biden and won in 2016 and 2024. The last four Black gubernatorial candidates to appear on ballots lost, but each contender ran in difficult areas and environments for their respective parties.

Three Black Republicans have lost in high-profile races in recent years, despite leaning heavily on their support of Trump. Former North Carolina Lt. Gov. Mark Robinson lost by nearly 15 points amid a sex scandal and other controversial comments in 2024, and former Virginia Lt. Gov. Winsome Earle-Sears lost by almost 16 points last year.

Kentucky Attorney General Daniel Cameron, once a protege of Sen. Mitch McConnell, lost to Gov. Andy Beshear, a rare popular Democrat in the state, in 2023. Shawn Wilson, Louisiana's Democratic two-term state transportation secretary, lost the same year.

Will Nevada elect a Black man?

Ford, the Nevada attorney general, will likely face a highly competitive race against incumbent Gov. Joe Lombardo in a state Trump lost in 2016 and 2020 but won in 2024. Ford made history in 2018 as the Silver State's first Black statewide elected official when he flipped the attorney general seat for Democrats.

During this race, Lombardo and his GOP allies have repeatedly spotlighted his Democratic foe's travel out of state, referring to him as "frequent flyer Ford" in attack ads. Reports say those trips have been mostly for professional conferences but also campaigning for former Vice President Kamala Harris.

"I recognize it for what it is. I've dealt with this the entirety of my political career," Ford told USA TODAY in July. "Nevadans don't countenance this type of nonsense, which is the reason why I've won statewide twice – including the last time by more than anybody else running statewide."

Demuth is unlikely to win in Minnesota over longtime Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar. Johnson, a Democrat in reliably red South Carolina, will also face a difficult electoral landscape.

Uptick in Black political participation this cycle

The current bumper crop of Black gubernatorial nominees pursuing higher office occurs at a time when Black representation is expected to plummet in Congress and state legislatures.

A Supreme Court ruling this summer gutted a key provision of the Voting Rights Act, which has allowed Republican-dominated states such as Texas to redraw their maps with fewer majority-Black or Latino districts in order to minimize Democratic-leaning seats.

"What's going on right now is you’re watching the greatest forms of political redlining that we have seen in generations," Moore said, referring to the practice of banks refusing to lend to homebuyers in certain areas, often heavily Black or Latino neighborhoods.

Black voters have responded with high turnout at the polls. A study by VoteHub, a nonpartisan organization offering political analysis, shows a surge in Black voter participation in Southern primaries.

'Voting rights gave you power:' The Voting Rights Act turns 60. Will its promise endure?

In four Black Belt states in the American South – Louisiana, South Carolina, Alabama and Georgia – average primary turnout was about 26% overall, but rose to 32% in majority-Black counties, a difference five times larger than the last midterm primaries in 2022.

Democratic strategist Nina Smith, a former senior adviser to Abrams' 2022 campaign for Georgia governor, said there's a heightened level of participation among Black Democratic voters, particularly in the South.

"There's a level of awareness and amongst our people that we are under attack," she said. "You can absolutely see a 'Black wave' of self-organizing that is happening."

Only 14 Black senators, elected or appointed, have ever served in the Senate. Barack Obama, a former senator from Illinois, became the first Black president, and Kamala Harris, a former senator from California, became the first Black vice president.

While more progress has been made in the House of Representatives, which has seen 189 Black members in total, Black candidates have struggled to win gubernatorial elections.

Speaking with USA TODAY, Moore acknowledged there is a pride the Black community has with Obama and the election of others, such as himself, but that voters cannot fall victim to believing those historic gains end the need for more inclusive leadership.

Before Moore makes a potential run for the White House, he wants more Black Americans to make history in governor's mansions after decades of work from voting rights activists.

"It's important that we're vigilant, and it's important that we do not relinquish or give up a political power that those who came before us, you know, worked for and fought for and died for."

news.title: Why Can’t Josh Shapiro Take a Hint?
news.text:
Pennsylvania’s governor with obvious 2028 presidential ambitions, Josh Shapiro, recently posted on the X platform that he is suing the Trump administration “to stop their unconstitutional attempt to change the rules and restrict mail-in voting.”

He then blathered on about “free, fair, safe, and secure elections” in his defense of a system that guarantees elections that are anything but free, fair, safe, and secure. To which conservative pundit and radio host Mark Levin responded, “You’re an idiot. You’re not going to be president. Your party hates you.”

You’re an idiot. You’re not going to be president. Your party hates you. https://t.co/jyk8SRikBm— Mark R. Levin (@marklevinshow) August 26, 2026

While Levin nailed it, some finer points need to be made as to why Shapiro can never be president. Spoiler alert: It’s because his party does indeed hate him.

Shapiro is well understood to be a practicing, observant, conservative Jew. He keeps kosher. When he was sworn into office as Pennsylvania’s governor, he did so by placing his hand on a Hebrew Bible that came from the scene of the murderous attack on Pittsburgh’s Tree of Life synagogue in 2018.

The Jewish news site, Forward, reported that when Shapiro campaigned for governor, “he proudly embraced his Judaism during the campaign.”

As a sitting governor, Shapiro became the target of an arson attack when Cody Balmer, who would later plead guilty to the crime, lit the fire that destroyed a portion of the governor’s mansion while Shapiro and his family were inside. The attack came in the early morning hours of Sunday, April 13, 2025, not long after the Shapiro family held a Passover seder.

According to the Associated Press, Balmer had “scaled an iron security fence in the middle of the night, eluded police and used beer bottles filled with gasoline to ignite the occupied Pennsylvania governor’s mansion.” He was charged with 22 counts of arson, aggravated arson, burglary, aggravated assault, 21 counts of reckless endangerment, loitering, and yes, terrorism. He now faces 25 to 50 years behind bars.

Police reports and a call from Balmer to 911 indicate that his motive for the crimes was his problem with the governor’s stance on Israel’s war in Gaza and “plans for what he wants to do to the Palestinian people.” The timing of the crime only reinforced this.

Shapiro has not backed off of his support for his culture, his faith, and the Israeli state. Like Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.), Shapiro has been consistently pro-Israel. He has been anti-Hamas. Though as a loyal Democrat, Shapiro has also been for a two-state solution, and he’s taken his shots at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

He called Netanyahu “one of the worst leaders of all time,” and he blamed the Netanyahu administration, at least in part, for conditions leading up to the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel and innocent Israelis.

This is a balancing act for the practicing Jewish Democrat politician who badly wants his party’s nomination for the presidency in 2028. He won’t turn his back on his faith, but he’s consistently looking for an avenue where he can align himself with a party he knows to be increasingly and more fundamentally antisemitic.

Coming up short

His approach thus far, though ineffective, has been to try to differentiate between Israel and its leadership, and to the extent possible, to de-emphasize something that until now he has showcased – his Jewish faith.

It hasn’t been working. In Shapiro’s own memoir, Where We Keep the Light, he wrote that when Kamala Harris was vetting him as a possible running mate in 2024, her team asked him if he had ever been “an agent of the Israeli government.” They asked him if he had ever spoken with an undercover Israeli agent.

Shapiro characterized the line of questioning as offensive and speculated that they focused on this because he was “the only Jewish guy in the running.” Still, ever the good Democrat soldier, he has consistently said on record that antisemitism was not why he got passed over for Gov. Tim Walz of Minnesota.

Jewishness aside, Shapiro has shown a willingness to be whatever the powers on the left want him to be if that’s what it takes to get the nod for 2028. It’s now pretty obvious that on the Democrat side in the race for president, elections are mere formalities. Shapiro knows that to become the nominee, the most important votes he gets will come from a cabal in the shadows that has the money and controls the agenda.

Selfies with Soros

This would explain why it’s not difficult to find photos of Shapiro cozying up to George Soros’s heir-apparent son Alex in that now famous New York penthouse apartment. That’s where Soros the younger has made a habit of taking photos with every mover and shaker in Democrat politics – trophies for his wall. This implied message is, “Look, these are the pols I own.”

In May, George Soros reported that he donated $30 million to fight antisemitism, but the New York Post and other news organizations reported that the leftist puppet-master is as much to blame as anyone for the recent surge in hate against Jews around the world. In making the announcement that the Soros’s Open Society Foundations (OSF) would dole out the money, Alex Soros said that, as a Jew, his father has been battling antisemitism his whole life.

The Post quoted New York State Assemblyman Kalman Yeger (D-Brooklyn), who said, “The Soros family claiming they will fight antisemitism is like the arsonist showing up with an empty fire extinguisher.”

OSF has funded Palestinian and pro-Palestinian groups for many years. Among those groups receiving OSF grants are Al-Haq, Al-Haq Europe, and Al Mezan. Both Al-Haq and Al Mezan are alleged to have ties to the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), which, along with Hamas, is a designated terrorist organization.

Soros’s Tides Center is a major funder for several leftist protest groups in the U.S., which have almost universally proclaimed their support for Hamas under the guise of being “pro-Palestine.” In the process, through their own messaging, they often tend to be unapologetically antisemitic.

Choosing to protest and celebrate on the anniversary of Oct. 7, and chanting things like, “From the river to the sea,” their “pro-Palestine” cover story often fails to hide their antisemitic foundations.

The 'Hamas wing' is in charge now

The unofficially dubbed “Hamas wing” of the Democrat Party is growing in size and influence. One of the party’s rising stars and new standard-bearers is Muslim New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who seems to speak more often about foreign affairs than about things everyday New Yorkers care about.

On the matter of the Israeli state, Mamdani won’t support the existence of Israel. In June, he told ABC’s Jonathan Karl, “I believe that any state that privileges one religion over the other is one that I can’t tell you I support, whether it be Israel or Saudi Arabia or anywhere else.”

On the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), Mamdani dehumanized the group as “monsters,” saying, “AIPAC, for whom the only thing more frightening than democracy being allowed to run its course is an end to genocide and Netanyahu’s wars.”

Mamdani is hardly alone in the Democrat Party. Another potential presidential contender for 2028, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) has been a consistently vocal critic of AIPAC and Israel. So has Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Ca.), Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), and Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.). While some of these politicians may have taken AIPAC money in the past, Politico reports that as the political winds have shifted in the Democrat party, the pols aren’t just distancing themselves from the Israeli cause; they’re running from it.

It should be noted that AIPAC tends only to donate to federal races, but that hasn’t stopped governors like Shapiro, Gavin Newsom (D-Ca.), and Andy Beshear (D-Ky.) from going public with their own proclamations that they have not and will not take AIPAC donations.

When they tell you who they are, believe them

The underlying message through all of this is that it’s not politically helpful to be seen as a Jew or pro-Israel in the Democrat Party. The rising stars are anti-Israel, and not coincidentally, a few are Muslims.

In the House, there are incumbents: Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.), Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.) Lateefah Simon (D-Ca.). New Muslim nominees for House races include Adam Hamawy (D-N.J.) and Aisha Wahab (D-Ca.).

In the Senate, the Democrats are hinging their hopes for a majority on Abdul El-Sayed to help the party hold onto a seat it hasn’t lost to a Republican since 1994. While El-Sayed won’t come right out and chant, “From the river to the sea,” at least not yet, he will signal what he feels he must to his base. We've covered El-Sayed extensively, and we will continue to do so, given the critical nature of the Michigan Senate race.

A Desperate El-Sayed Campaign Is Now Tapping the Old Soviet Propaganda Playbook

Like Mamdani, he refuses to say whether Israel has a right to exist. When a man rammed a truck into Temple Israel in West Bloomfield, Mich., El-Sayed said all of the perfunctory things in terms of condemning antisemitism, but then he undermined all of that by saying, “Hurt people do hurt people,” seemingly finding some excuse for the attack.

news.title: Trump says he’ll visit Pentagon, rather than Ground Zero, for 9/11 ceremony
news.text:
President Donald Trump will appear at the Pentagon to mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, instead of visiting Ground Zero in New York City. 

Asked about why he would not be commemorating the anniversary in his hometown, Trump told reporters Friday, “Because I’m going to the Pentagon.” 

Vice President JD Vance is instead expected to attend the event in New York City, according to a senior administration official. Other officials will attend a ceremony in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, on the day, the official added.

The New York Times first reported that Trump would travel to the Pentagon on 9/11, writing Thursday that the president had initially wanted to go to New York City but decided against it when organizers would not allow him to speak during the Ground Zero program, which traditionally does not permit speeches. 

The White House has denied that claim, with White House communications director Steven Cheung calling the report “FAKE NEWS” in a post on X Friday. 

A senior administration official also told reporters Friday that the report was “false” but would not explain further. 

“As a proud New Yorker, President Trump has spoken about his own experiences watching the horrific events of September 11, 2001,” White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement. “On the 25th anniversary of this tragic day, the President will remember those who were killed at the hands of evil terrorists, honor their loved ones, and pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line to rescue their fellow Americans.”

Trump visited the Pentagon on 9/11 last year before traveling to New York City to spend the evening at a New York Yankees game that honored the victims of the attacks. 

He did attend the ceremony at Ground Zero in 2024, appearing at the event where his presidential opponent, former Vice President Kamala Harris, and then-President Joe Biden were also in attendance. Trump had last gone to the New York City ceremony in 2016, but did visit a fire station and police precinct in the city in 2021. 

During his first term, Trump spent the anniversaries at the Pentagon in 2017 and 2019 and went to Shanksville, Pennsylvania, in 2018 and 2020.

news.text:
On Friday’s broadcast of MS NOW’s “The Moment,” Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed responded to a question on why he won’t fully disassociate with Hasan Piker by declaring that “this campaign is not about a streamer in California.”

Host Katy Tur asked, “It’s emotional, just as it was emotional in 2024 when Arab Americans stayed home and did not vote for Kamala Harris because of the war in Gaza, and cost her, arguably, the state of Michigan, even though Democrats were arguing Donald Trump’s going to be a whole lot worse. And he has been, in many ways. So, if you have Jewish voters in Michigan, I’ll say Dana Nessel is one of them, who are worried about your association with Hasan Piker, why keep him so close? Or why not fully disassociate yourself with him, especially when Michigan is so tight? Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) only won by 22,000 votes.”

El-Sayed answered, “So, let me speak to a couple of points here: Number one, I endorsed the vice president on the day after she became the nominee. I did not agree with the administration’s position on Gaza, but I understood that Donald Trump would be worse. So, I am calling on leaders from all of the communities under the Democratic umbrella to recognize that Mike Rogers is an existential threat to everything we believe in when it comes to our democracy. Number two, this campaign is not about a streamer in California. This campaign is about affordability in Michigan. This campaign is about the ability to have healthcare.”

Tur cut in to say, “The streamer in California does campaign with a lot of Democrats. So, he’s not just a streamer.”

El-Sayed responded, “This campaign is about the challenges Michiganders face, and I get that, in the media, it’s a lot easier to pick up one person and be like, this is what this is about. But this is why a lot of people get so frustrated about politics and political media, because it doesn’t actually speak to the challenges they face. Look, I did a whole interview –.”

Tur then cut in to say, “It’s not just the media, and I reject that framing. It’s — 6 in 10 Americans don’t know who he is. And I’m not saying he’s the most important person in the world, but when you have a state like Michigan, where, again, Elissa Slotkin only won by 22,000 votes, is it worth potentially losing the few votes you need to win?”

El-Sayed replied, “10 in 10 Americans agree that they can’t afford the things that they need in their life. So, if folks want to make this about a streamer in California, they’re welcome to do that. But I’m focused on Donald Trump, I’m focused on addressing the affordability crisis, I’m focused on getting you healthcare, and that’s what I’m going to stay focused on.”

news.title: Trump Rebukes New York Times Reporter Over Claim He Would Skip 9/11 Memorial Service
news.text:
Donald Trump lashed out at a New York Times report, attacking reporter Maggie Haberman after the paper said he was not expected to attend the 25th anniversary commemoration of September 11 at Ground Zero in Manhattan because he had been told he could not deliver remarks.

His post came just hours after a U.S. military judge ruled Friday that confessions allegedly made to FBI agents by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind of the 9/11 attacks, are inadmissible and cannot be used against him at trial.

According to The Times, Trump had sought to speak at the National September 11 Memorial and Museum, with members of his team reportedly making advance visits before the idea was discouraged because of the museum’s commitment to nonpartisanship.

Trump fired back on Truth Social, writing: “Maggot Hagerman, the Fake Reporter from The Failing New York Times, an unattractive person both inside and out, and who knows less about me than most reporters on the beat (She’s a SCAMMER!), made up a story that on September 11th, I’m not going to the World Trade Center, in New York City, because they won’t let me make a speech, and I’m going to the Pentagon in D.C., because I’m a featured speaker.”

The former president was referring to Maggie Haberman, the longtime New York Times journalist who has often been the target of his criticism over reporting that cites people familiar with his views and decision-making.

Trump also insisted he did not need a speaking role, saying he “would love not to speak, because I’m speaking all the time,” and adding that September 11 is “a day to remember the victims, and their beautiful family members.”

He went on to call Haberman “a PHONY,” accused her of stalking him, and claimed that his lawsuit against The New York Times would prove his allegations.

“If she were ever forced to reveal her ‘sources,’ you will find out they either don’t exist, or didn’t say what she reported,” Trump wrote. “She’s been falsely writing about me for years — she’s a stalker, and should be forced to turn over any and all money that she’s made through her fake reporting on me.”

Haberman has yet to publicly comment on Trump’s post. Our News Outlet has reached out to The New York Times for comment. 

The paper claimed Trump will mourn the victims for a second consecutive year in a ceremony at the Pentagon because he has not been allowed to give a speech, The New York Times reported. 

Trump wanted to give remarks at The National September 11 Memorial and Museum and had even gotten his team to make advance visits. 

But multiple sources said that the museum’s ultimate goal is to avoid any partisanship at the ceremonies, with politicians banned from speaking since 2012. 

Vice President JD Vance will represent the Trump administration at the New York ceremony instead, while ex-Presidents Bill Clinton, Barack Obama and George W Bush are expected to attend. 

Trump will return to Washington from the Republican Party’s midterm convention in Texas the two days prior to September 11.

As he did last year, Trump will give a speech at the Pentagon’s ceremonies, where politicians remain welcome to give an address.

He will then leave the country for Ireland to visit his golf course where the Irish Open is being held.

His flight would be significantly easier on local air traffic going out of Joint Base Andrews in Maryland than from any of the New York-area airports. 

In a statement to the Times, White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly emphasized a remembrance of the victims but made no reference to the President’s specific plans. 

Our News Outlet has reached out to the White House for further comment. 

The President also commemorated September 11 at the Pentagon last year, in a ceremony that was moved into the internal courtyard after the assassination of Charlie Kirk.

Trump pledged to always honor those who died on that day. 

‘We will defend the nation they served, the values they upheld and the freedom for which they died,’ he said. 

‘We will support our troops, we will protect our families, and we will preserve the American way of life for every future generation.

‘We will build taller, grow stronger, fight harder and soar higher, and together we will go forward as one people with one heart, one faith, one flag and one glorious destiny under almighty God,’ he added.

Trump did go to New York afterward, as he attended a Major League Baseball game between the New York Yankees and Detroit Tigers at Yankee Stadium. 

The last time Trump attended the Ground Zero ceremony was in 2024, when he was in the same company as Kamala Harris, as the two shared an awkward handshake. 

Trump and Harris appeared cordial at Ground Zero as they met for a second time in 24 hours following the first debate between the two, even sharing the handshake which was facilitated by Republican-turned-Democratic former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg.

Harris stood alongside President Joe Biden during the ceremony while Bloomberg acted as a buffer separating the current administration from Trump and his running mate Vance. Trump allegedly complimented Harris’s debate performance.

The attendance by Trump, Biden and Harris is rare and marks one of the few times the former president and current president have been in the same space.

The three would not be in the same space again until Trump’s second inauguration in Washington just four months later. 

This week, the trial date for Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and three others accused plotters was set for June 5, 2028 at the US naval base in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba.

Mohammed, also known as ‘KSM,’ was considered one of Al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden’s top lieutenants before he was captured in March 2003 in Pakistan.

Prosecutors have already excluded statements that Mohammed made after his capture when he was held by the CIA in overseas prisons and subjected to brutal treatment including waterboarding before his transfer in 2006 to Guantanamo, the Times reported.

But the trial judge Lieutenant Colonel Michael Schrama has concluded that Mohammed’s subsequent interrogations in 2007 at Guantanamo were also inadmissible.

‘The prosecution has failed to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that Mr. Mohammad´s statements to the FBI were voluntarily given,’ Schrama wrote in his ruling, which was not immediately released to the public. The Times said its unclassified contents were confirmed by several lawyers who had seen it.

A spokesman for the US military court did not immediately respond to an AFP request for comment.

Schrama cited an ‘unbroken continuation of the CIA´s psychological conditioning and severe coercion,’ and also found that FBI agents intentionally failed to tell Mohammed that he had a right to be silent and to consult a lawyer.

Prosecutors can appeal the ruling.

Mohammed’s trial has been repeatedly delayed and a plea deal that would have seen the death penalty taken off the table was withdrawn last year following protests from the relatives of some victims of the 9/11 attacks.

Much of the legal jousting in the 9/11 defendants’ cases has focused on whether they could be tried fairly after having undergone torture at the hands of the CIA.

news.title: Trump's having a midterm party. But it may not be a hot ticket
news.text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump is throwing a big party to rally the GOP for the midterms, but not every candidate may be happy to get the invitation.

That's because some Republicans warn that it could backfire in battleground races.

Trump took the unprecedented step this year of organizing a midterm convention, his party’s first, as he seeks to put his stamp on the election and stoke GOP enthusiasm, which has lagged behind Democrats.

Republicans will convene in a Dallas sports arena on Sept. 9 and 10 to hear speeches from Trump and Vice President JD Vance. Organizers are pitching it as an opportunity to build party unity, hone their message and reach voters who may not have tuned in. Yet some in the party say there is no upside for candidates in close races to leave the campaign for an event in another state with a president floundering in polls ‒ and there are questions about who will attend.

“If I was in office running for re-election I would not be taking time going to Texas,” said former Michigan GOP Rep. Fred Upton. “I’d be connecting with voters. I’d have events . . . at home.”

The convention comes just after Labor Day, as the campaign season kicks off in earnest, requiring candidates to take time away from talking to voters less than two months before Election Day. Being too closely tied to Trump also could be problematic for candidates in tight races. Just four in 10 voters approve of the president in the Real Clear Politics average of recent polls.

“I can’t think of very many candidates whom it would help,” GOP strategist Charlie Black, who has worked on multiple presidential campaigns, said of a Trump-focused convention.

Two other Republican strategists, including one who worked in the current Trump administration, and a Republican member of Congress aligned with Trump questioned the value of the convention in interviews with USA TODAY. Their views ranged from seeing the gathering as pointless to potentially harmful for battleground candidates. The lawmaker said candidates will only benefit if they hold fundraisers in Dallas.

USA TODAY contacted eight GOP Senate candidates in top battleground states – North Carolina, Georgia, Michigan, Maine, Alaska, Iowa, Texas and Ohio – to ask if they are planning to be at the convention. Representatives for Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers and Ohio Sen. Jon Husted confirmed they are attending, but spokespeople for most of the candidates did not respond to multiple inquiries.

Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine was among the candidates whose representatives ‒ both from her campaign and Senate office ‒ did not respond to questions about whether she plans to attend the convention.

Collins has worked to distance herself from Trump as she seeks a sixth term representing a state that has voted Democratic in every presidential election since 1988. Collins did not attend an event Vice President JD Vance held recently in Brewer, Maine to tout the administration's efforts to combat state-level fraud.

'We're going to defy history'

Organizers say they expect a packed convention.

Republican National Committee Chair Joe Gruters said there is a "pretty full list of candidates and elected officials" attending, including nearly two thirds of GOP senators and 80 House members who already have indicated they’ll be in Dallas.

When it comes to marquee Senate races, Gruters said he’s not sure which candidates will be there, though.

“I don’t know,” he said, adding: “It’s probably a mixed bag.”

The convention will help bring the party together after a series of tough primaries and get the base motivated, Gruters said. If candidates think they’re better off skipping the event and campaigning in their districts “that’s great,” he added.

“But if you want to be part of history… we’re going to defy history and we’re going to win these midterms and this is the official start of us planting our flag in our efforts to do that,” Gruters said.

Cost is another potential factor. The National Republican Congressional Committee is asking House members to contribute a minimum of $25,000 to attend as a party fundraising effort, according to a source familiar with the plan. Gruters said that arrangement is "an internal deal they have with their caucus" but he suspects many House members won't have to pay to attend.

The RNC released a convention program this week. Vance is speaking Sept. 9, while Trump is giving the keynote address Sept. 10. No other speakers have been officially announced, and Gruters said they may not be until the day of the event.

Instead, the program lists different topics that will be covered, such as border enforcement, tax cuts and healthcare affordability. Time is reserved each night for a “candidate showcase.”

'Continuing to hug Trump'

A relatively small number of races could decide control of the House and Senate. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 advantage in the Senate and 218-212 advantage in the House. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates 69 House races and 10 Senate races as competitive on some level, with the rest considered solid Republican or Democratic seats.

Upton, who served for 36 years in a Michigan swing district before opting not to seek re-election in 2022, said Republican candidates in swing seats won't benefit from attending the convention. He said they instead need to show some independence from Trump.

“Otherwise, the tidal wave will be pretty big,” said Upton, who voted to impeach Trump and later endorsed Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris.

Gruters said Trump can deliver the voters the GOP needs to win, and the convention will help amplify his message.

Many GOP candidates already are tightly bound to the president. They often owe their nominations, at least in part, to Trump’s endorsement and may be unwilling to risk his wrath by skipping the convention or breaking with him in other ways.

Trump's early endorsement helped propel Senate candidates in battleground states such as Iowa, Michigan and North Carolina to win their primaries, while the president came in late to help deliver the Texas Senate nomination to Attorney General Ken Paxton. Trump stayed out of the Georgia Senate primary, but the candidate who won, Rep. Mike Collins, is a strong ally of the president.

Southern Methodist University political science professor Calvin Jillson said Trump isn’t helping the GOP ticket, pointing to his low approval rating. But candidates know he is prone to lash out at those who cross him.

“So I don’t think people feel like they have much of an option other than continuing to hug Trump,” he said.
