news.title: As Midterm Elections Approach, Republican Candidates Weigh How Closely To Align With Trump
news.text:
NEW YORK (AP) — “AIR FORCE VETERAN. SMALL BUSINESSMAN. TRUMP CONSERVATIVE.”

The all-caps headline on Texas Republican congressional candidate Carlos De La Cruz’s website used to align him with President Donald Trump. Not anymore.

“NATIVE TEXAN. AIR FORCE VETERAN. SMALL BUSINESSMAN. PROVEN CONSERVATIVE,” it reads now.

De La Cruz’s campaign rejected any suggestion he was backing away from the president, whose knack for mobilizing his loyalists remains critical for Republicans in this fall’s midterm elections. The overwhelming majority of Republicans on the ballot this fall are embracing Trump despite his dismal approval ratings, an unpopular war with Iran and lingering inflation.

However, as the two-month sprint to Election Day begins, a small collection of Republican candidates have quietly begun to distance themselves in subtle ways from Trump now that they’ve won contested primaries in which his endorsement was often the most coveted prize. The shift is easy to miss, often only a few words or new pictures. And Republicans insist there is no shift at all.

Mike Marinella, a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee, called it a “manufactured storyline.”

“President Trump and House Republicans have delivered historic results for the American people, and our candidates are eager to take that record directly to voters alongside the President on the campaign trail,” he said.

But from California to Texas and Kentucky to Alaska, candidates in recent weeks have tweaked their campaign messaging to downplay their connection to Trump. A handful of others have highlighted their opposition to his policies.

It’s an extremely delicate balance for vulnerable Republican candidates, who must expand their appeal beyond Trump’s MAGA base to win in the general election this fall, but are also afraid to trigger a backlash from Trump or his hard core supporters if they create too much distance.

Trump’s Unpopularity Could Weigh Down His Party

Most candidates are still wrapping their arms around Trump.

Republican allies of the president argue there is little upside for candidates to turn away from Trump, despite his weak polling numbers. Democrats will try to cast every Republican running as a Trump acolyte, regardless of their actual stances, they said, and midterm successes typically depend on turning out base voters. Trump remains the Republican Party’s best motivator.

“The whole Republican brand is that we’re aligned with Trump so you gain nothing from it,” said Jason Roe, a Republican who advises Rep. Tom Barrett, who is fighting for reelection in a competitive mid-Michigan district race.

It is typical for candidates from both sides to tweak their messages after primary elections. Some Democrats, for example, have begun pitching themselves as moderates after highlighting endorsements from progressives like Sen. Bernie Sanders during their primaries.

Still, the slight shift among at least a half-dozen Republican congressional candidates could signal the beginning of a more significant move within the party as the weight of Trump’s unpopularity with the general public comes into view at a critical moment. Just 33% of adults approve of Trump’s job performance, according to Associated Press-NORC polling from July. And Trump gets relatively poor ratings on his handling of the economy, immigration and foreign policy.

Meanwhile, Trump will not make it easy for vulnerable Republicans to avoid him. As voters typically begin paying much closer attention to politics after Labor Day, the president will headline a two-day Republican convention in Dallas as he urges voters to act as if he were on the ballot.

“The problem that we have is they say that Trump does great when he’s on the ballot, but when he’s not on the ballot, his people don’t come,” Trump said as he recently stumped in South Carolina.

“So what I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot,” he went on. “Just say that I’m on the ballot one more time.”

Shifting Emphasis Moving Into The General Election

A number of Republicans have removed or downplayed references to Trump from their websites after winning their primaries.

Eric Flores, a former assistant U.S. Attorney and Texas Army National Guard infantry captain running against Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez Jr. in South Texas, once featured “SUPPORT PRESIDENT TRUMP’S AGENDA” as No. 2 in his list of priorities on his campaign homepage.

That item has now been replaced with “ LOWER THE COST OF LIVING,” a top issue for voters. Trump does not appear anywhere else on the website, aside from a list of endorsements that previously appeared on the homepage but has been moved to a separate page.

Flores’ campaign declined to comment.

In Kentucky, Ralph Alvarado, running to represent the overwhelmingly Republican 6th Congressional District, removed all references to Trump from his campaign homepage, as well as a photo of the two of them together after winning his primary in May. He now promises to offer “INDEPENDENT LEADERSHIP” after previously running as an “AMERICA FIRST FIGHTER.”

NBC News first reported the changes to Alvarado’s website. Campaign manager Andy Westberry noted Trump’s photo still appears elsewhere in a media gallery. “The socialists are going to have to do a lot better than this nonsense to win this district,” he said in a statement.

Some changes do not mean Trump has been erased.

While De La Cruz no longer touts himself as a “TRUMP CONSERVATIVE” at the top of his homepage, a video that is embedded lower down features the Air Force veteran speaking at a Trump rally.

He still calls himself a “TEXAS TRUMP CONSERVATIVE” on his bio page and lists “Supporting President Trump’s America First Agenda” as among his priorities on a “Mission” page.

But the bio section has also been tweaked. It once described him as “ready to be President Trump’s wingman in Congress.” That section now says he is running because he “believes America needs more servant leaders and fewer corrupt politicians” and “because he’s not finished serving the country he loves.”

De La Cruz campaign manager Jordan Pawlicki said in a statement that, during the primary, several candidates were claiming the president’s endorsement, so the campaign “put it front and center.”

“Carlos is honored to have President Trump’s support, which is why the President is featured prominently across our website,” Pawlicki said.

Republicans Downplay Any Changes To Their Messaging

In Nevada, Republican congressional candidate Marty O’Donnell’s website featured Trump prominently in June. The very first thing visitors saw was a pop-up with a large picture of Trump and a smiling O’Donnell standing side by side. The words “President Trump endorsed Marty O’Donnell” were written beneath the image.

Two months later, the photo does not appear on the website. O’Donnell’s campaign said the photo was not intentionally removed; the change was simply the standard rotation of the “splash page.”

O’Donnell adviser Keith Schipper noted that O’Donnell, a music composer best known for his work on the “Halo” video game series, has not deviated from his steadfast support for Trump.

“Republicans are embracing President Trump on the campaign trail because they know he is the key to getting his voters out in November,” Schipper said. “The president has delivered on the agenda he promised voters in 2024 and Republicans are smartly using it to win this year.”

There was another subtle shift in Alaska’s House race, where Republican Rep. Nick Begich is running for reelection.

In June, he highlighted his relationship to Trump on the homepage of his website: “Alongside President Trump, we have made great gains for Alaska, putting us on a path to self-determination and generational success.”

This week, nothing in that section has been changed, except for the opening line that previously mentioned Trump. Now, that line reads, “We have delivered for Alaska, putting us on a path to self-determination and generational success.”

Begich’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

Some Are Emphasizing Their Independence

Rep. Mike Lawler, a New York Republican who represents a district carried by Kamala Harris in the last election, appeared on stage with the president during a rally in his district just three months ago. But does he want Trump to return before Election Day?

“If he comes back, that’s fine, but ultimately this race is going to be decided by my record and my vision,” Lawler said in an interview.

Lawler supported Trump’s so-called “big, beautiful bill,” but he’s quick to highlight policy differences, especially on taxes. Trump does not appear on Lawler’s campaign website.

On Thursday, Tom Tiffany, the Republican candidate for governor in Wisconsin who is closely aligned with Trump, publicly criticized the president’s decision to sign an order renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America” as part of his trade war with Canada.

“I believe the Great Lakes are the Great Lakes and should stay Lake Superior, Lake Michigan, Lake Ontario,” he said, according to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel.

Earlier this week, he came out against Trump’s plan to import cheaper ground beef in an effort to reduce prices.

Others want distance from Trump’s unpopular war with Iran.

In Michigan, Rep. Barrett, who flipped a Lansing-area district two years ago, has been highlighting his vote against Trump’s war in Iran on the campaign trail as he competes against William Lawrence, a self-described democratic socialist.

Barrett this year has repeatedly broken ranks with Republicans to join Democrats in voting for the War Powers Resolution to rein in Trump’s military campaign in Iran. And he has been promoting those votes, promoting a recent town hall with constituents, by saying he would “be having a discussion about the War Powers Act and my efforts to place congressional limits on the war in Iran.”

Roe, the Republican who advises Barrett, said the vote was not about some major break from Trump but a difference over a policy-specific issue. Barrett served in the U.S. Army for over two decades.

“He’s willing to be at odds with the White House on this issue,” Roe said. “It’s important to him.”

Associated Press writer Joey Cappelletti reported from St. Joseph, Michigan.

news.title: Trump says he'll visit Pentagon, not NYC, to mark 25 years since 9/11
news.text: Washington — President Trump said he will not be in New York City next month to mark 25 years since the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks because he's going to the Pentagon instead. Asked by a reporter Friday why he won't commemorate the event in his hometown of New York, Mr. Trump said, "Because I'm going to the Pentagon." Vice President JD Vance will visit New York on Sept. 11, a White House official said. "The vice president is still traveling to NYC and all three sites will be represented with administration officials in attendance," a White House official said, referring to the attack sites in Manhattan and the Pentagon and the field in Pennsylvania where United Airlines Flight 93 crashed.Mr. Trump, a Queens native, last attended the annual Ground Zero commemoration ceremony in 2024 while running for president, along with then-President Joe Biden and then-Vice President Kamala Harris. He didn't attend the ceremony last year, although he attended a New York Yankees vs. Detroit Tigers game in New York City that honored the victims. "As a proud New Yorker, President Trump has spoken about his own experiences watching the horrific events of September 11, 2001," White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said. "On the 25th anniversary of this tragic day, the president will remember those who were killed at the hands of evil terrorists, honor their loved ones, and pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line to rescue their fellow Americans."The New York Times first reported the president wouldn't attend the Manhattan ceremony.During his first term in office, the president didn't attend the Manhattan ceremony, instead honoring the victims at the Pentagon or at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, or both. In 2021, he visited New York City police officers and firefighters in Manhattan. Mr. Trump attended the Manhattan ceremony in other years, including in 2016, when he was running against Hillary Clinton. Former President Bill Clinton and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton will attend the commemoration ceremony in Manhattan next month, a Clinton spokesperson confirmed to CBS News. Former President George W. Bush and former first lady Laura Bush also plan on attending, according to the Bush Presidential Center.
news.summary: The White House said President Trump will "pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line."
news.author: Emma Nicholson,Kathryn Watson

news.title: Trump backs out of 9/11 anniversary ceremony after organizers refuse to let him give a speech
news.text:
President Donald Trump is skipping the official New York City ceremony commemorating the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks after organizers denied his request to deliver a speech.

Trump’s team had initially signaled to New York officials that the president planned to attend the landmark milestone at the World Trade Center site, with advance teams conducting site visits in recent weeks. 

However, plans were abruptly altered after memorial planners reminded the administration of the event's long-standing policy prohibiting political figures from addressing the crowd, according to the The New York Times.

The National Sept. 11 Memorial and Museum has barred all elected officials and politicians from speaking at the Ground Zero ceremony since 2012. 

The rule was established following years of political friction surrounding the site's reconstruction, with organizers and victims' families agreeing that the annual gathering should remain strictly solemn, nonpartisan, and centered entirely on the reading of the 2,977 victims' names by their surviving loved ones.

Instead of attending the Manhattan ceremony, Trump will mark the milestone at the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia—which was also struck during the 2001 attacks—where he will be permitted to deliver formal remarks.

Vice President JD Vance will attend the Ground Zero commemoration in New York on behalf of the administration, joining a roster of expected dignitaries including former Presidents Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, and Barack Obama.

The White House did not directly address the reports regarding the speech request, but issued a statement affirming Trump's connection to the tragedy.

“As a proud New Yorker, President Trump has spoken about his own experiences watching the horrific events of September 11, 2001,” White House deputy press secretary Anna Kelly said.

 “On the 25th anniversary of this tragic day, the President will remember those who were killed at the hands of evil terrorists, honor their loved ones, and pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line to rescue their fellow Americans.” 

Trump last attended the Ground Zero ceremony in 2024 during the presidential campaign, standing silently alongside Vance, then-President Joe Biden, Vice President Kamala Harris, and former Mayor Michael Bloomberg without delivering public remarks.

Travel logistics also factored into the scheduling shift, with the president slated to depart from Joint Base Andrews for an overseas trip to Ireland the following day.
news.summary: The US president will instead commemorate the 25th anniversary of the terror attacks at the Pentagon
news.author: Phoebe Tonks

news.title: Democrat in Striking Distance of Flipping State Trump Won by 23 Points—Poll
news.text: Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith held a 6-point lead over Democrat Scott Colom in a new poll of the Senate race in Mississippi, a state that favored President Donald Trump by more than 20 points in the 2024 election. Mississippi is not ordinarily seen as a competitive state for Democrats; it’s been one of the most consistently conservative states across the country in recent elections. But Democrats like Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg have signaled support for Colom, a district attorney, as the party hopes to expand the battleground. Due to its large Black population, Mississippi has been a high-floor, low-ceiling state for Democrats; they regularly receive more than 40 percent of the vote in the Magnolia State but have struggled to win a majority due to its intense racial polarization. But Democrats hope that a favorable environment, as well as a possible surge in Black turnout across the South, could make this race more competitive than expected. Jake Monssen, Hyde-Smith’s campaign manager, told Newsweek the poll was “partisan” and “fielded to produce the headlines and fundraising appeals they wanted.” He said that with the “resources and organization” that campaign has, voters will “hear the truth” about Colom. “Our internal numbers look strong. We will not let up until the polls close on November 3, and we are confident Senator Hyde-Smith will once again earn the support of a majority of Mississippi voters,” he said. Colom wrote in a statement provided to Newsweek that the poll "makes clear that when Mississippians hear about both of us, I win." Hyde-Smith’s Narrow Lead in New Poll The new poll from Data for Progress, a left-leaning polling firm, suggested the race could be more competitive than expected for such a red-leaning state. Hyde-Smith held a 6-point lead over Colom, 44 percent to 38 percent, with independent candidate Ty Pinkins receiving an additional 7 percent of the vote. She held onto that 6-point lead in a scenario without Pinkins on the ballot, leading Colom 47 percent to 41 percent, according to the poll, which surveyed 1,018 likely voters from August 5 to August 15. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. The poll found that Hyde-Smith is not viewed particularly well in the state, with a net favorability rating of -10 points. Fifty percent of respondents said they viewed her unfavorably, while 40 percent viewed her favorably. Colom had a stronger net favorability rating but was much less known in the state, with 28 percent of respondents saying they view him favorably and 15 percent unfavorably, according to the poll. President Donald Trump, however, is still viewed positively in the state, although by a narrow margin, with 51 percent viewing him favorably compared to 47 percent unfavorably. On the informed ballot, when respondents heard a short biography about each candidate, Colom and Hyde-Smith were tied at 40 percent. How Conservative Is Mississippi? Mississippi is generally not considered a competitive state, and Republicans have enjoyed a strong advantage there. Trump performed especially well there in 2024, winning 60.9 percent of the vote compared to former Vice President Kamala Harris’ 38 percent. It was the first time a Republican presidential candidate got more than 60 percent of the vote since 1984. In 2020, Trump won by about 17 points, 58 percent to 41 percent. He carried the state by 18 points in 2016, 58 percent to 40 percent. Republicans also easily carried the state by 12 points in 2012 and 13 points in 2008. But the state has been closer in some other races. In 2020, Hyde-Smith won by 10 points over Democrat Mike Espy, 54 percent to 44 percent. She won by less than 8 points in 2018, about 54 percent to 46 percent. Its gubernatorial race was also close in 2023, when GOP Governor Tate Reeves defeated Democrat Brandon Presley by only about 3 points. Roger Wicker won by a stronger margin in 2024, defeating Pinkins, who is now running as an independent, by more than 25 points. Could Democrats Flip Mississippi This Year? Although the state is a tough lift for Democrats, some prominent leaders have suggested the race could be worth targeting in this year’s midterms. Schumer earlier in August told Semafor that he does view the race as a “long shot,” but that Colom is a “tough prosecutor who’s won elections in a tough district” and that Hyde-Smith is “extremely weak.” “We’re always looking to expand the map with candidates who fit their states,” he told the news outlet. Buttigieg, viewed as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, told MS Now this week he is supporting Colom. “I’ve been paying a lot of attention to uphill races that we could actually win. And yeah, in almost any other year, and with almost any other candidate, a race like this would seem out of reach. But what I see in Scott Colom, and why I wanted to get involved in this race, is there’s a real chance here,” he told the outlet. Colom has also sought to make the case he can win, writing in a Facebook post Thursday, “I’ve been saying it for months: Mississippi is competitive and we can win in November.” Democrats believe they will be able to compete in more conservative states due to Trump’s declining national approval rating. His popularity has waned as Americans sour on his economic policies like tariffs as the cost of living remains high, and the unpopular war in Iran has also become a sore spot for many voters. Turnout among Black voters could be key. Some Democrats see signs of it surging in the South after the Supreme Court’s ruling in Louisiana v. Callais, in which a majority of justices ruled to weaken Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. A VoteHub analysis found "Black Belt" states did see a primary turnout increase after the Callais decision, though it’s unclear how that will translate to the general election. Independent polling on the race is limited. Prediction markets favor Republicans to hold the seat. Hyde-Smith had a 93 percent chance of winning on Kalshi and a 95 percent chance on Polymarket as of Friday afternoon. Elections forecasters also view the race as less competitive, with the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball both classifying the race as solid or safe for Republicans. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gabe Whisnant and Edward T. Cummins.
news.summary: Democrats are hoping Scott Colom can make Mississippi's Senate race competitive in November.

news.title: Donald Trump Skipping 9/11 25th Anniversary Event After Being Told He Can’t Give a Speech: Report
news.text:
President Donald Trump is reportedly planning to skip Ground Zero’s 25th anniversary ceremony for the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center in part because he was barred from giving a speech.
Ahead of the event, Trump’s team conducted visits to the site of the attack in Manhattan, New York, often referred to as Ground Zero, the New York Times reported on Friday, August 28, citing “four people with knowledge of the events.” They signaled to officials in New York and Washington that the president intended to visit Ground Zero himself and hoped to speak at the September 11 ceremony. However, politicians have been banned from speaking at the site since 2012 in an effort to keep it nonpartisan.
Trump, 80, is now expected to attend a ceremony at the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia — which also came under attack on September 11, 2001 — according to the outlet.
Another reason for his attendance at the Pentagon instead of Ground Zero is that Trump is planning to travel to his golf course in Doonbeg, Ireland, the following day, and it’s easier to leave from Joint Base Andrews in Maryland than the tri-state area airports, the NYT reported.
Vice President JD Vance is expected to represent the White House in New York.
“On the 25th anniversary of this tragic day, the President will remember those who were killed at the hands of evil terrorists, honor their loved ones, and pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line to rescue their fellow Americans,” White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement.
The statement continued, “As a proud New Yorker, President Trump has spoken about his own experiences watching the horrific events of September 11, 2001.” (Trump, a native New Yorker, spoke about the September 11 attacks during his 2016 presidential campaign.)
The president and First Lady Melania Trump marked the September 11 anniversary at the Pentagon last year.
“In America we take blows, but we never buckle. We bleed, but we do not bow, and we defy the fear, endure the flames and emerge from the crucible of every hardship stronger, prouder and greater than ever before,” Trump said in his speech at the time. “Last year we were a dead country, now we have the hottest country anywhere in the world.”
Trump last attended a September 11 memorial event in NYC during the presidential race in 2024, when he joined then-president Joe Biden, then-vice president Kamala Harris and other officials at Ground Zero.
Several other politicians are expected to attend the 25th anniversary memorial at Ground Zero, including former Mayor Rudy Giuliani, former President Bill Clinton and his wife, Hillary Clinton, former President George W. Bush and his wife, Laura Bush, and former President Barack Obama, the NYT reported.

news.title: 12 Years Ago, Barack Obama Stepped Up to the Podium in a Tan Suit
news.text:
NEED TO KNOW

President Barack Obama’s tan suit moment in 2014 sparked outsized scrutiny from his critics and conservative media, who spent a whole news cycle decrying the outfit as “unpresidential” and more akin to a Hamptons party getupThe outfit became one of the most memorable controversies of Obama’s presidency and a lasting cultural momentObama has since embraced the moment, most recently poking fun at the fashion choice on Larry David’s Life, Larry, and the Pursuit of Unhappiness

Few outfits have sparked political backlash and controversy quite like former President Barack Obama’s tan suit.

Twelve years ago, on Aug. 28, 2014, Obama got dressed in a light beige suit and a gray striped tie to attend a press briefing at the White House. The fashion choice immediately gained traction with his critics, who said the look was “unpresidential,” lacked “seriousness” and looked to be something one might wear to a Hamptons party.

While it’s perhaps most common to see male politicians wearing dark-colored suits for their official appearances, there’s no dress code or protocol that barred this break from the norm. Former Presidents Ronald Reagan and Bill Clinton had also worn markedly similar outfits in comparable hues before the scrutiny Obama faced for the same look.

The infamous tan suit unexpectedly became one of the most memorable — and overblown — controversies of Obama’s eight years in the White House, often cited as an example of the disproportionate scrutiny Obama faced as the nation’s first Black president.

Since then, the outfit has taken on a life of its own, and Obama himself has come to own the moment in creative ways.

Never miss a story — sign up for PEOPLE’s free daily newsletter to stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories.

In 2024 — on the 10th anniversary of what he called “Suitgate” — the former president poked fun at then-Vice President Kamala Harris’ tan suit, heavily reminiscent of his own, in a post on Instagram. Obama then shared a side-by-side photo of himself and Harris in their respective beige getups.

“How it started. How it’s going. Ten years later, and it’s still a good look! IWillVote.com,” Obama wrote in the caption.

More recently, in August 2026, Obama made a special cameo in the series finale of Larry David’s Life, Larry, and the Pursuit of Unhappiness and reimagined the tan suit debacle as David’s fault. The episode cast David as Obama’s fictitious adviser who ultimately helped the former president choose the controversial suit.

After spilling a drink on Obama’s navy blue suit — the one the president intended to wear to the press conference in the satirical show — David tries to cover his tracks by directing Obama instead to the tan suit. After all, it’s “casual Friday,” David’s caricature of himself justifies.

Once the suit is on, David reassures Obama with a hilariously ironic line: “People are going to be talking about this for a long, long time.”

At the dedication ceremony for the Obama Presidential Center in June, some high-profile attendees wore tan suits in honor of the former president’s silliest controversy, including late-night veterans Stephen Colbert and David Letterman.

news.title: Democrats Lead Republicans in 5 States Trump Won by Double Digits: Map
news.text: Democrats are mounting competitive Senate and gubernatorial campaigns in several states that President Donald Trump carried by double-digit margins in the 2024 presidential election. The competitive contests in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas have raised questions about whether Republicans, who hold both the House and Senate majorities, face mounting political headwinds ahead of the 2026 midterms and whether Democrats can capitalize on them. Trump’s Slipping Approval Rating Costas Panagopoulos, a political science professor at Northeastern University, told Newsweek that "presidential approval and the state of the economy are both strong predictors to outcomes in congressional races in midterms. The president's sagging rating on both of these metrics are making races in these states more competitive than we'd expect.” Trump's approval ratings have raised concerns among some Republicans as the party heads into the 2026 midterms. Nationally, 35 percent of voters approve of Trump's job performance while 59 percent disapprove as of August 27, leaving him significantly underwater with a net approval rating of -24, according to Civiqs' rolling online tracking poll of registered voters. The survey has garnered 126,377 responses since January 20, 2025, when Trump was inaugurated for a second term. An August 25 Economist/YouGov poll found 35 percent of Americans approved of the president's job performance, with a net approval rating of -26. Compared to a similar poll during the same point in his first term, his net approval rating was -9 and former Democratic President Joe Biden’s -12. Aggregators like RealClearPolitics show Trump with a 40 percent approval rating and 57 percent disapproval, while the Silver Bulletin puts his approval rating at 38 percent. A new Strength in Numbers/Verasight poll fielded August 14-19, which surveyed 1,514 U.S. adults ages 18 and older, found Trump underwater on all 12 issues it tracks, as border security—his last positive rating—slipped to −5. The poll had a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 2.6 percent. Alex Patton, owner of strategic public affairs firm Ozean Media, told Newsweek via email that the current climate is not a result of just one factor; rather it is being driven by a “toxic soup of mega-trends of economic factors, inflation, gas prices, grocery prices, the job market, the President's record-low approval numbers (especially with Independents), the quagmire in Iran, and, in some cases, terrible candidates.” He described the current political environment as “terrible, gawd-awful” for the GOP, “with maybe the only win being the stock market, and the stock market is not the economy.” Hans Noel, a professor of government at Georgetown University, told Newsweek that “Trump has involved himself even more in the midterms, so voters are even less likely to not think of him when they vote.” Trump’s 2024 Election Victory Trump won the 2024 election against then-Vice President Kamala Harris, securing 312 Electoral College votes to Harris' 226 and winning the national popular vote. Trump carried 31 states overall, including 24 by double-digit margins, and clinched all the swing states. His margins among the states he won by double digits ranged from Ohio, which he won by 11.2 percentage points, to deeply Republican Wyoming, where he won by 45.8 points. Other states he won by double digits included Alaska, Florida, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, South Carolina, Tennessee and West Virginia. Republicans also regained control of the Senate in 2024, flipping Democratic-held seats and securing a majority in the chamber, while maintaining control of the House of Representatives. At the state level, Republicans entered 2025 holding a majority of governorships nationwide. “At the end of the day, in 2024 Donald Trump was a rising tide lifting all Republican boats, but in 2026 he is a falling tide lowering all Republican boats from sea to shining sea," Mark Jones, a politics professor at Rice University, told Newsweek. 2026 Midterms Political experts note that losses by the party controlling the White House are common in midterm elections. However, they also caution against viewing the 2026 midterms solely as a referendum on Trump, noting that while the president's approval ratings and the national political environment are likely to play the largest role in the elections, factors such as candidate quality, local issues and state-specific dynamics are also helping shape a number of competitive races. “Democrats lost 63 House seats and six Senate seats in the 2010 midterm, then another 13 House seats and nine Senate seats in 2014, both under Obama,” Matt Klink, owner and president of Klink Campaigns, told Newsweek, noting that those elections occurred under presidents who were more popular than Trump is now. He added that Republicans also faced significant setbacks during Trump's first term, noting that “Republicans lost 40 House seats in 2018, Trump's own first midterm.” Many analysts suggest that Trump's standing with voters is giving Democrats opportunities in states that would normally be difficult targets. Doug Gordon, a Democratic strategist at Upshift Strategies, told Newsweek, “Trump's historic unpopularity and the fact that the majority of voters believe that he has failed to deliver on his promise to lower prices have given Democrats an excellent opportunity to compete in states that might have otherwise been out of reach,” while cautioning that there is still a long way to go before Election Day. Not all analysts view the races primarily through a national lens, though. Tim Hagle, an associate professor in the Department of Political Science at the University of Iowa, noted that “midterms also tend to be more about local issues,” though he said campaigns can sometimes become nationalized, a strategy he believes both parties are pursuing this cycle. Still, some observers say the Senate map looks markedly different from it did just a few months ago. Reflecting on the shifting landscape, Jones told Newsweek that “six months ago, the best Democrats looked likely to be able to achieve in the U.S. Senate was a reduction of the Republican advantage to 51-49 for the final two years of Donald Trump’s term in office, but today they have a clear pathway to a majority, one which only requires them to win three of the current six toss up races.” Noel from Georgetown University said, “In general, the Democratic Party has been trying to find a way to break through to voters they have lost to Trump, and midterm elections are great place to experiment with that.” Voters will determine the balance of power in Congress and a series of state races in less than 75 days. Alaska Trump easily carried Alaska in the 2024 presidential election, winning 54.5 percent of the vote to Harris' 41.4 percent, a margin of about 13.1 percentage points. Despite Alaska's Republican tilt at the presidential level, Democrats have remained competitive in statewide races, aided in part by the state's ranked-choice voting system. Alaska has voted Republican in every presidential election since 1968, with comfortable margins for Trump in the past three elections. The state has not elected a Democratic governor since Tony Knowles left office in 2002, and the state's last Democratic U.S. senator, Mark Begich, left office in 2015. Alaska Senate Race The Senate contest has emerged as one of Democrats' more plausible pickup opportunities in 2026. Republican Senator Dan Sullivan is seeking another term, while Democrats are backing former Representative Mary Peltola, who won a special House election in 2022 before losing reelection in 2024. Dave Hopkins, a political science professor at Boston College, told Newsweek, “Senate Democrats are benefiting from a successful recruiting year for Senate candidates, particularly in Alaska where Mary Peltola was the strongest possible Democratic nominee.” Polling shows a tight race. A Data for Progress survey of 605 likely voters in Alaska found that in the first round of voting, no candidate received an outright majority, with 47 percent saying they would vote for Peltola compared to 41 percent for Sullivan. In Alaska, all candidates appear on a single ballot regardless of party, and the four with the most support advance to the general election. Three percent said they would vote for Gerald Heikes, another Republican candidate, while 5 percent were undecided. In the final round of ranked-choice voting, however, Peltola led Sullivan by 6 points, 53 percent to 47 percent, according to the poll. It surveyed 605 likely voters in Alaska from July 28 to August 4, 2026 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. An Alaska Survey Research poll put Peltola ahead of Sullivan 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent in the final round. It surveyed 1,371 likely voters from August 2-5, 2026, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. However, a June New York Times/Siena College poll found Sullivan ahead 47 percent to 45 percent, with about 5 percent undecided. The poll of 593 Alaskan voters was conducted between June 15 and 19 and has a margin of error of plus or minus 4.9 percentage points. The Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball rate the race as a “toss up.” While Alaska's open governor's race is expected to be competitive, major election forecasters still give Republicans an edge. Ohio “Ohio is the one to watch,” Klink told Newsweek. Patton and Hagle also noted that the state represents Democrats' strongest pickup opportunity of the cycle. Trump carried the state by about 11 percentage points in 2024, an improvement over his 2020 and 2016 performances, when he won by about 8 points each time. But Ohio was viewed as more competitive for Democrats not long before. Former President Barack Obama narrowly carried Ohio in 2008 and 2012. It has shifted as Trump performed well among the state’s working-class voters. Despite that Republican trend, Ohio has a history of electing Democrats statewide. The state's most recent Democratic senator was Sherrod Brown, who served from 2007 until his defeat by Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024. Brown is now seeking a return to the Senate in a 2026 race against Republican Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill the remainder of Vice President JD Vance's term. Ohio Senate Race Brown, who represented Ohio in the Senate for 18 years, is now facing Husted for the full-term Senate seat. An August Fox News poll found Brown leading Husted by 8 points, 53 percent to 45 percent, with about 2 percent undecided. Brown leads among independents in Ohio by 38 points, 66 percent to 28 percent for Husted. The poll of 1,008 registered Ohio voters was conducted August 6-10. A Wedgewood Poll of 800 likely voters conducted between August 11 and 13 found Brown with 48 percent to Husted’s 44 percent. About 8 percent of voters were undecided. The poll has a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. Forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball view the race as a toss-up. Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifted it from Lean Republican earlier in June after Brown and Husted formally won their parties’ nominations. Ohio Governor’s Race The state's most recent Democratic governor was Ted Strickland, who served from 2007 to 2011. Ohio has elected only Republican governors since then, including current Governor Mike DeWine, who won reelection in 2022 but is now term-limited. Democrat Amy Acton, the former director of the Ohio Department of Health who gained statewide prominence during the COVID-19 pandemic, is facing Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, a former presidential candidate and DOGE member. Polls point to a close matchup. The same Wedgewood poll found an even tighter race for the governor’s mansion, with Acton ahead by 1 point, 47 percent to Ramaswamy’s 46 percent. Seven percent of the participants were undecided. A Fox News poll conducted August 6 to 10 among 1,008 registered voters put Ramaswamy ahead, 50 percent to 48 percent. The survey has a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. Tulchin Research found Acton leading 46 percent to 44 percent in a survey sponsored by John Kulewicz, the Democratic candidate for Ohio attorney general. The survey, conducted July 29 to August 4 among 660 likely voters, had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. A New York Times/Siena College poll of 601 likely voters, conducted June 15 to 28, had the candidates tied at 47 percent. Its margin of error was plus or minus 4.7 percentage points. An AARP survey conducted June 14 to 16 by Democratic firm Impact Research and Republican firm Fabrizio, Lee & Associates gave Acton a 47 percent to 44 percent lead among 800 likely voters. Its margin of error was plus or minus 3.5 percentage points. The Cook Political Report rates the race as a toss-up after moving it from the Lean Republican column in a July update. Explaining the shift, the forecaster wrote that “it’s an inescapable law of politics: Money can only propel a campaign so far when its candidate’s flaws act as an anchor.” Texas Texas has backed Republican presidential nominees in every election since 1980, but Democrats hope 2026 will offer one of their best opportunities in years to compete statewide. Trump carried Texas by 13.7 percentage points in 2024, defeating Harris 56 percent to around 42.5 percent. Texas has not elected a Democrat to statewide office since 1994, making it one of the nation's longest-running Republican strongholds. Democrats have repeatedly targeted the state as demographic shifts and population growth have reshaped its electorate, but they have fallen short in a series of closely watched campaigns, including Beto O'Rourke's 2018 Senate bid against Ted Cruz. Texas Senate Race The GOP's decades-long hold on Texas statewide offices will be tested in November, with the Senate race between Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic state Representative James Talarico nearly deadlocked. Surveys show both Paxton, who is endorsed by Trump, and Talarico, who has served as a state representative since 2018, holding narrow leads at different points in the campaign. The matchup follows Paxton's defeat of longtime Senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary in late May. “Texas is the wild card: with Ken Paxton defeating John Cornyn in the GOP primary, Democrats inherited a nominee carrying real legal baggage. Right now, the race is less about James Talarico and more about Ken Paxton, his money problems, and his personal foibles,” Klink said. Jones also spoke about Paxton’s reputational and legal history to Newsweek, stating, “Candidate quality is an issue for Republicans in a few instances, and is having an especially negative impact on Republican prospects in Texas where Ken Paxton arguably is the weakest major statewide Republican candidate in modern Texas GOP history.” Hopkins said his “scandal-ridden past seems to be a serious liability.” In 2023, the Republican-controlled Texas House impeached Paxton on 20 articles. The Texas Senate acquitted him. Paxton has repeatedly dismissed the impeachment and other allegations as politically motivated. Accusations of bribery and infidelity also circulated during the impeachment trial, with one of the articles stating that Paxton “benefited from Nate Paul’s employment of a woman with whom Paxton was having an extramarital affair.” His wife, state Senator Angela Paxton, filed for divorce in 2025, following “recent discoveries” and citing “biblical grounds.” Polls appear to flip-flop on who is leading, as a recent Emerson College Polling/Nexstar Media poll of 1,000 likely Texas voters puts the Senate race in a near dead heat, with 47 percent backing Paxton and 46 percent supporting Talarico. About 5 percent are undecided and 2 percent back a different candidate. The poll was conducted August 9-11 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. A Fox News poll of 1,006 registered Texas voters found that 51 percent back Talarico and 48 percent Paxton, with 1 percent undecided. The survey was conducted July 23-27 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. The Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball rate the race as “toss up.” Iowa Iowa was viewed as a battleground for much of the 2000s, with Obama carrying the state by about 10 points in 2008 and 6 points in 2012. But Trump performed well in the state in each of his presidential bids, winning by 10 points in 2016, 8 points in 2020 and 13 points in 2024. Iowa Senate Race Republican Representative Ashley Hinson is going against Democratic state Representative Josh Turek in the Iowa Senate race. They are running to succeed Republican Senator Joni Ernst, who chose not to run for reelection. Democrats haven't secured a Senate seat in the state since Tom Harkin's election in 2008. Turek is a two-time Paralympic gold medalist and state House member, first elected in 2022. Obama endorsed him in a late-July video, while Trump has endorsed Hinson, who was first elected in 2020 after serving in the state House and working as a journalist. “I'm not sure Iowa's Senate race is as close as some polls show, but we do have three competitive House races too, so Democrats are hopeful,” Hagle from the University of Iowa said. An Emerson poll this month found Hinson with a slight lead, 47.5 percent to 45 percent. She was viewed favorably by 44 percent of respondents and unfavorably by 40 percent, while Turek was viewed favorably by 42 percent and unfavorably by 27 percent. It surveyed 712 likely voters August 2-4 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.7 percentage points. A Fox News poll of 1,003 Iowa registered voters found Turek leading Hinson 50 percent to 46 percent, with 4 percent undecided. The poll was conducted June 23-27 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. The Cook Political Report updated the race's rating from leaning Republican to a toss-up on August 20. Sabato’s Crystal Ball rates the race as “leans Republican.” Polling averages suggest a competitive contest. RealClearPolling's average shows the race nearly tied, with Hinson at 47 percent and Turek at 46.3 percent. Iowa Governor’s Race Republican Governor Kim Reynolds, who has led the state since 2017, is not seeking reelection. The last time a Democrat won Iowa’s governorship was in 2006, when Chet Culver was elected. Culver lost his reelection in 2010 to Republican Terry Branstad, and Republicans have been in office ever since. Iowa State Auditor Rob Sand, a Democrat, is going up against Republican businessman Zach Lahn in the state's open governor's race. “For Republicans, Lahn is basically an unknown. His victory in the primary was a surprise, likely to him as well, and he's had to work on increasing his name ID,” Hagle told Newsweek, contrasting him with Sand’s name recognition given his state role. “Sand has built a brand as a ‘numbers-guy auditor’ that plays well with independents,” Klink added. A Suffolk University poll released Wednesday found Sand ahead of Lahn 48 percent to 44 percent among 500 likely Iowa voters, with 9 percent undecided. The survey, conducted August 20-23, has a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. Sand's advantage has held across a string of surveys this summer, though its size keeps shifting. An Emerson College Polling survey put Sand up to 48 percent, while Trump fell to 43 percent. Two percent of respondents said they would vote for someone else, while 7 percent were still undecided. The survey polled 712 likely voters August 2-4 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.7 percentage points. A survey from The New York Times and Siena University, conducted among 600 likely voters June 15-27, showed Sand up a single point, 48 percent to 47 percent. Meanwhile, a Fox News poll showed Sand up 9 points, 53 percent to 44 percent. Beach Research and Shaw & Company Research conducted it from June 23-27 among 1,003 registered voters. The Cook Political Report rates the race lean Democratic, while Sabato's Crystal Ball places it in the toss-up category. Kansas Kansas has been a reliable state for the Republican Party at the presidential level for decades. Trump carried Kansas by 16.2 percentage points in 2024, defeating Harris 56.2 percent to 40 percent. The state has not voted for a Democratic presidential nominee since Lyndon B. Johnson's landslide victory in 1964. Kansas’ Governor’s Race Kansas' open governor's race has emerged as one of Democrats' more surprising opportunities in 2026. Democrat Cindy Holscher is seeking to succeed term-limited Governor Laura Kelly, one of the few Democratic governors in a state Trump carried by double digits. Republicans have nominated Ty Masterson and are favored by most forecasters, with the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball both rating the race as lean Republican. There hasn’t been much public polling of the general election, but early polls show a competitive race. A recent Global Strategy Group survey found Holscher leading Masterson by 1 percentage point, though the result was within the poll's margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. The Democratic sponsored poll of 600 likely voters was conducted between August 13 and 16. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Sam Wilson.
news.summary: Democrats are making states Trump won by double-digit margins in 2024 competitive ahead of the 2026 midterms.
news.author: Mandy Taheri

news.title: Trump 'Skipping 25th Anniversary 9/11 Ceremony' in New York to Visit His Golf Course in Ireland
news.text:
Donald Trump is skipping the upcoming memorial commemoration in Manhattan for the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attack on the World Trade Center, RadarOnline.com has learned.

The president will instead mark the grim milestone in a much smaller way, before jetting off to his golf course in Ireland for the Irish Open.Donald Trump Will Not Speak at Manhattan MemorialTrump's decision to pass on the ceremony reportedly came after he was told he would not be able to speak at the hallowed site now known as ground zero. 

According to The New York Times, Trump had planned to attend, and staffers made advance visits to the site to prepare for his appearance. 

He also wanted to speak at the event. However, the National September 11 Memorial and Museum has prohibited politicians from delivering speeches at the annual commemoration since 2012 in an effort to keep the event nonpartisan and focused solely on victims and their families.

After learning he would not be allowed to speak, the 80-year-old canceled his plans, and will instead pay tribute at the Pentagon, site of the second terror attack on Sept. 11, 2001.

Vice President J.D. Vance is expected to represent the White House at the New York event. Former Presidents Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, and Barack Obama are also expected to attend, along with former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani.Donald Trump Set to Tee Off OverseasThe president's travel plans reportedly also played a part in the decision to avoid Manhattan. Trump is scheduled to depart for his golf course in Doonbeg, Ireland, the day after the anniversary. Leaving from Joint Base Andrews in Maryland would cause fewer disruptions than departing from New York or New Jersey. 

Trump last attended the ground zero ceremony in 2024, alongside then-President Joe Biden and then-Vice President Kamala Harris.

news.title: Trump Backed Out of 9/11 25th Anniversary Ceremony Because Organizers Wouldn’t Allow Him to Give a Speech: Report

President Donald Trump is reportedly skipping the New York City ceremony commemorating the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacksThe president will instead mark the anniversary at the Pentagon after officials at the New York memorial denied his request to make a speech, according to The New York TimesVice President JD Vance is expected to attend this year’s N.Y.C. ceremony in Trump’s place

President Donald Trump is reportedly skipping the New York City ceremony commemorating the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks after officials denied his request to make a speech, according to The New York Times.

Organizers at the National Sept. 11 Memorial and Museum have barred politicians from speaking since 2012, according to the Times and an Associated Press report from that time.

The White House did not acknowledge the Times’ reporting on the request to make a speech when reached for comment by PEOPLE on Friday, Aug. 28.

“As a proud New Yorker, President Trump has spoken about his own experiences watching the horrific events of September 11, 2001,” White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement. “On the 25th anniversary of this tragic day, the President will remember those who were killed at the hands of evil terrorists, honor their loved ones, and pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line to rescue their fellow Americans.”

Instead of the Ground Zero ceremony, the longtime New Yorker will attend the annual commemoration at the Pentagon, as he did last year. During the 2024 election, Trump attended the New York ceremony alongside then-President Joe Biden and his campaign rival, Vice President Kamala Harris.

Vice President JD Vance is expected to attend this year’s ceremony in Manhattan, and administration officials will also be present at the Flight 93 Memorial outside Shanksville, Pa.

Former Presidents Bill Clinton, George W. Bush and Barack Obama are expected to attend the New York event at the site of the Twin Towers, as are former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, former first lady Laura Bush, and former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani, according to the Times.

Prior to the 25th anniversary of the deadliest attack on the United States since Pearl Harbor, Trump will be in Texas for a Republican convention ahead of November’s midterms. Then, on Sept. 12, he leaves for Ireland to attend the Irish Open at one of his golf courses.

Trump opened his remarks at the Pentagon in 2025 by memorializing Charlie Kirk, a longtime ally and political operative who was assassinated the day before during an event at a Utah college. He announced he planned to give Kirk the Presidential Medal of Freedom posthumously.

Later that evening, he attended the New York Yankees game in the Bronx.

In 2012, Joe Daniels — the then-president of the 9/11 Memorial & Museum — told the AP that their decision to limit politicians’ remarks was intended to honor “the victims and their families in a way free of politics.”

Trump, who made his name and grew his businesses for decades in New York, was in the city when the Twin Towers were attacked on Sept. 11, 2001. He called into a New Jersey television station that day and claimed that one of his buildings would now be the tallest in lower Manhattan.

news.title: New Data Shows Gen Z Regrets Voting For Trump
news.text:
New data from public opinion research firm Navigator found that 31 percent of Generation Z said they regret voting for President Donald Trump in the 2024 election.

Generation Z showed more regret about their voting choices compared with 28 percent of Millennials, 20 percent of Generation X, and 10 percent of Baby Boomers, who all said they regretted voting for Trump, according to the data, compiled from several surveys taken between June 4 and July 27. Alternatively, 69 percent of Generation Z said they did not regret voting for Trump, compared with 72 percent of Millennials, 80 percent of Generation X, and 90 percent of Baby Boomers.

In addition, Trump has the lowest approval rating among Generation Z, with only 33 percent of voters saying they either strongly approve or somewhat approve of the way he is handling his job as president. Trump had a 38 percent approval rating among Millennials, 39 percent among Generation X, and 41 percent among Baby Boomers. (RELATED: Nearly One-Third Of Gen Z Steers Clear Of Car Insurance, Survey Finds)

Furthermore, Generation Z is the most pessimistic about the direction of the country, with a net of -42 saying the country is headed in the right direction compared with Millennials (net -35), Generation X (net - 34), and Baby Boomers (net -27), the same data shows. Fifty percent of voters between the ages of 18-44 said they disapproved of Trump’s handling of the economy but also do not trust Democrats on the issue.

Notably, Trump’s war against Iran continues to be deeply unpopular, with 52 percent of respondents saying they either strongly or somewhat oppose the military action.

Gen Z regrets Trump support and is midterm motivatedhttps://t.co/GTdzo9y48M— The Hill (@thehill) August 28, 2026

Tina Tang, director of polling and analytics at Navigator, discussed the data with The Hill.

“Young Americans are telling us that politics is deeply important to who they are, but it doesn’t mean they’re happy with the current political system, or that they’re even optimistic about the direction of the country as a whole,” Tang said.

“Young Americans are disproportionately represented among people who are dissatisfied with Trump and the economy. It doesn’t mean they’re flocking to one party or another.”

“Gen Z is not a group that’s hard to understand. Politics are important to them, but they are also pessimistic about the economy right now,” she continued.

Navigator identified Generation Z voters as individuals who were born between 1998 and 2008.

Data from the Pew Research Center shows Trump received 45 percent of the vote among individuals between 18 and 49 in 2024, compared to former Vice President Kamala Harris, who received 52 percent of the vote among the same age group.

The Navigator data was compiled from several polls conducted between June 4 and July 27.

news.title: Why some Democrats running in red states are pushing away Biden, Harris
news.text:
With less than 70 days until the midterm election, some Democrats running in the most conservative areas are sending a clear message to former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris: stay out of their races.

In Iowa, Democratic Senate nominee state Rep. Josh Turek -- who has welcomed the support of former President Barack Obama and has twice won a seat in a district that voted for President Donald Trump -- was asked if Harris should campaign for him. He simply said "No."

Also in Iowa, Democratic gubernatorial nominee Rob Sand told Politico "no thanks" to the idea of Biden or Harris campaigning for him. He also said Harris should not run for president in 2028, arguing the country needs "new leadership."

Alaska Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola recently distanced herself from Harris after her political action committee backed Peltola in a fundraising email.

"Mary isn't seeking endorsements from anyone from the Lower 48 -- her focus is and always will be Alaska," Peltola's campaign told The New York Times.

The blunt rejections, coming within days of each other in two states Trump carried by double digits in 2024, underscore a reality for Democrats: candidates fighting for independent and moderate Republican voters increasingly see the party's brand and most recent presidential ticket as a liability.

The Senate races are particularly vital to Democrats, who are looking take control in the chamber where the GOP has a slim majority.

Putting 2024 in the rearview

Democratic strategist James Carville told ABC News that the Democratic Party is "just ready to move on from 2024" as "everybody’s scarred by it." He added that this phenomenon is not necessarily new, saying that "no Republicans" were looking for Mitt Romney's support in 2014 -- two years after Romney lost the 2012 election to Obama.

Carville added that Biden's prostate cancer diagnosis could be a limiting factor for his campaigning, and that "Democrats like Harris fine. They just don't find her particularly inspirational."

After the start of the Iraq War, when President George W. Bush's favorability ratings were down, he stuck to events with minimal press coverage in areas that were Republican strongholds, according to news reports at the time during the 2005-2006 midterm cycle.

During the run-up to the 2008 election, he barely appeared alongside John McCain, mostly holding private fundraisers out of the public eye.

Ashley Etienne, Harris' former communications director, said voters are disillusioned with the political establishment as "the Democratic Party's brand is in the tank."

Democratic strategist Matt Corridoni of the political organization, The Bench, which backs Peltola and Turek, said the candidates are signaling a break from the status quo.

"It doesn’t really make sense to have someone who was our nominee last cycle be on the trail for you," Corridoni said. "That represents the past. It represents partisan institutions."

A longtime Democratic donor who raised money for Harris' 2020 presidential campaign and asked not to be identified told ABC News, "Kamala showing up in Pennsylvania -- or Alaska, or Iowa -- she's not going to get the same enthusiasm as when she walks into South Carolina or New York City."

The donor added that Democrats need middle America appeal, "and you don't get the middle with Kamala."

The Harris team declined to comment on the recent remarks by Sand, Turek and Peltola. ABC News reached out to Biden's team for comment, but didn't hear back by the time of publication.

The political calculus varies by district

Some say it all depends on the voters a candidate is trying to reach.

"Somebody like Mary Peltola who has a very good chance of flipping the Alaska Senate seat has to be very careful and strategic … that means ensuring she’s not bringing surrogates into the state or using their voices online in ways that could potentially turn off some of her very persuadable voters," said Adrienne Elrod, who served as Harris' senior adviser and spokesperson in 2024.

"There are some places where [Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez] is in demand, and there are some places where she's not. A lot of it just depends on the makeup of the target demographic that you're going for," Elrod added.

Some Democrats have actively sought Biden and Harris' support.

Former Biden White House aide Dan Koh, who is running to replace Rep. Seth Moulton in Massachusetts, told ABC News he asked Biden and Harris to endorse him. He said voters have told him they would vote for him because he has been backed by Biden.

"I've seen their integrity firsthand … I do not believe in running away from people that I believe in, that I've worked with," Koh said. "And I'm fortunate that the electorate has agreed."

Chris Jones, who's running to replace Republican incumbent French Hill in Arkansas, recently received Harris' endorsement, along with the support of Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.

Asked whether Harris' backing is helpful in his red district and about Sand and Turek's remarks, Jones told ABC News, "campaigning is hard … every candidate is different, every constituency is different, and every moment is different."

Implications for 2028

The Harris donor said that if Turek, Sand or Peltola win in November, it could encourage other potential 2028 presidential contenders to further distance themselves from Harris and move more toward the center.

Red and purple state Democrats such as Beshear, Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona and Buttigieg of Indiana -- all potential 2028 presidential contenders -- have recently campaigned in Iowa, showing an effort to reach voters well beyond the Democratic base. Beshear has campaigned for Sand; Kelly has campaigned for Turek and Buttigieg has campaigned for both Turek and Sand.

"If any one of them win," the donor said of Turek, Sand and Peltola, "you will see the [Pennsylvania Gov. Josh] Shapiros and the Beshears … maybe you'll have a Mark Kelly who will even move a little bit more center where they're going to say, 'look, we can't win this election by just winning blue states, we need to win purple states.'"
news.summary: Some Democrats running in the reddest areas are sending a clear message to former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris: stay out of their races.

news.title: Nevada Governor Endorsed Data Centers Days After AI Investor Donated $1 Million
news.text:
Three days after a prominent artificial intelligence investor and his wife donated $1 million to a political action committee boosting Nevada Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo’s reelection campaign, Lombardo publicly endorsed the state’s booming data-center buildout. A week later, the PAC collected another $1 million from the wife of a developer building those facilities in Nevada, according to campaign finance records reviewed by The Lever.

The revelation comes as the driest state in the nation grapples with data centers’ enormous resource demands. Fueled by $340 million in state tax abatements since 2021, Nevada has roughly 70 data centers in operation, under construction, or being planned. But amid new research suggesting the industry’s expansion could triple the state’s energy demands and consume as much water annually as roughly 150,000 households, cities and counties across the Silver State have begun issuing moratoriums on new data centers.

The matter could become a pivotal election issue. Lombardo’s Democratic opponent, Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford, has criticized the incumbent’s stance on data centers and just sued the federal government over cuts to its already strained Colorado River allocation. (Lombardo also supports the lawsuit.)

“Now we know why Joe Lombardo says he’s ‘wholeheartedly in support of data centers: He’s bought and paid for by them,” Ford told The Lever in response to the data center-related donations. “Taking care of his and Trump’s ‘billionaire friends’ at Nevadans’ expense is standard operating procedure from Lombardo. I’m running for Governor to pause and audit data centers’ tax breaks and block them from raising our costs, because I fight for working Nevadans — not data center billionaires, like Joe Lombardo.”

On May 11, Better Nevada PAC, a political action committee supporting Lombardo, received $500,000 from Ben Horowitz, cofounder of venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, and another $500,000 from Ben’s wife, Felicia. Andreessen Horowitz, also known as a16z, has invested in numerous AI and data center companies, and Horowitz has long been a prominent political donor. Horowitz and his business partner Marc Andreessen both donated $2.5 million to Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, and Horowitz later donated another $2.5 million to former Vice President Kamala Harris’ campaign. 

Three days after Lombardo received the Horowitzs’ donations, he posted a video on X stating, “I support data centers because they bring jobs, investments, and economic growth to Nevada.” 

On May 21, the Better Nevada PAC received another $1 million from Jessica Roy, wife of Rob Roy, who founded Switch, a data center development company currently building facilities in Nevada. Switch has received millions of dollars in tax abatements, according to The Nevada Independent. Andreessen Horowitz is also a major Switch investor.

On June 25, Lombardo also received $5 million from the Republican Governors Association, a nonprofit dedicated to electing GOP governors that has received at least $8.5 million from people and companies invested in AI and data centers since January 2025. Ken Griffin, founder and CEO of investment firm Citadel, donated $3 million; and Paul Singer, CEO of Elliott Investment Management, donated $2.5 million. Both Citadel and Elliott are heavily invested in AI and data centers. 

This month, Lombardo told the Latin Chamber of Commerce that data centers could be a “new gold rush,” if the proper guardrails are in place. Standing beside President Donald Trump at a different event, he also voiced his support for Trump’s “billionaire friends” because “those billionaire friends provide jobs. And unless you take care of them, those jobs are absent.”

Lombardo’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

“An Opportunity to Diversify Nevada’s Economy”

In a June op-ed for the Reno Gazette Journal, Lombardo argued that Nevada can pioneer a model for states to effectively work with data centers, calling them “an opportunity to diversify Nevada’s economy, strengthen our workforce and position our state as a national leader in technology and innovation for decades to come.” Data centers will bring jobs and investments to the state, he wrote, as long as guardrails prevent residents from paying higher utility bills and protect the state’s water resources. 

He added that data centers are “known to use massive amounts of water… and raise electricity costs for surrounding communities,” but claims that “it isn’t happening in Nevada.”

A January report from the Desert Research Institute, a science nonprofit, found that in 2024, data centers consumed 22 percent of the state’s electrical generation, an amount that the institute predicted could grow to 35 percent by 2030. The same report found that the state’s current development plans could result in data centers consuming up to 16 billion gallons of water annually, according to calculations by The Lever — enough for roughly 150,000 households a year. 

“Assuming the highest level of efficiency, the water needed annually for data center cooling under the projected load growth from NV Energy is more than 14,940 times the water needed for a single household, close to 17 times the water needed for an 18-hole golf course, and approximately six times the water needed for an alfalfa farm,” the authors wrote.

Then in May, NV Energy, the state’s largest energy provider, issued a report stating that Nevada’s future energy demands will nearly triple due to data centers.

Earlier this month, NV Energy sued Tract, a data center developer building two massive facilities near Reno, claiming that it is trying to pass infrastructure and energy costs on to consumers. According to NV Energy, Tract is trying to move the matter to a private court to evade public criticism.
news.summary: The revelation comes as the driest state in the nation grapples with data centers’ enormous resource demands.

news.title: Trump Trade war dooming Republicans in key swing state he narrowly won
news.text:
Democrats suffered major disappointments in Pennsylvania in 2024 when Donald Trump narrowly defeated Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris and three-term Democratic Sen. Bob Casey Jr. was voted out of office. But Democratic strategists are feeling optimistic about Pennsylvania in the 2026 midterms. According to the Philadelphia Inquirer, Trump's trade war with Canada is hitting the Keystone Star hard — and the pain is having both political and economic fallout.

"President Donald Trump says he's holding Canada accountable for 'ripping off' the United States through unfair trade practices," journalists Andrew Seidman and Lizzie Mulvey report in the Inquirer. "But by imposing new tariffs on Canadian goods and prompting retaliation from one of America's largest trading partners, U.S. businesses and consumers could face higher costs, analysts said — including in key electoral battlegrounds like Pennsylvania."

The Keystone State, according to Seidman and Mulvey, "sold $13.4 billion in goods last year to Canada — its largest export market."

"About $2 billion worth of those goods, or 16 percent, will be subject to higher tariffs — some as high as 50 percent — starting September 8 after Canada this week announced new levies, according to an Inquirer analysis of trade data," the reporters note. "Some of the state's top exports facing new tariffs include raw aluminum, lumber, and passenger vehicles."

Lauren Swartz, CEO of the nonprofit World Affairs Council of Philadelphia, is sounding the alarm about the effects Trump's trade war with Canada will have in her state. 

Swartz told the Inquirer, "When we think about what that means for Pennsylvania, it's going to be loud. My sense is the rhetoric that we're hearing, and the fact that it's already being labeled a trade war, is that both countries are reserving the right to escalate the level, the percentage of tariffs, as well as the scope of goods that will fall under the new trade war. So, it will expand."

The tariffs' effect on Pennsylvania is a major focus of centrist Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro, who is seeking reelection and has been leading GOP nominee Stacy Garrity in polls. 

Manuel Bonder, a spokesman for Shapiro's campaign, told the Inquirer, "Donald Trump's reckless tariffs are a tax on Pennsylvanians — and Gov. Shapiro has been fighting back against them from Day 1. This president has raised costs for families, screwed over our farmers, and shut down markets for businesses — all with Stacy Garrity's 100 percent support." 

Shapiro's attacks on Garrity and Trump appear to be working.
